figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: Token analysis, BFT, and applications. a : Semantic composition of low-confidence tokens inside Group A (sparse-low) and Group B (dense-low). b : 4096-token trace illustrating one sparse-low window (Group A) and one dense-low window (Group B). c : BFT applies token- and sample-level loss adjustments. d : BFT-generated biomedical profiles are encoded by a text embedding model for downstream representation tasks.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure combining plots, schematic workflows, and model architecture.

- **Panel a:** Bar chart of **token composition (%)** comparing **Group A sparse-low windows** and **Group B dense-low windows**. Categories include interchangeable expressions, common vocabulary, biomedical entities, and causal/reasoning chains. Group A appears enriched for interchangeable/common vocabulary tokens, while Group B appears enriched for biomedical entities and causal/reasoning chains.
- **Panel b:** Line/trace plot of **4096-token response confidence**, with highlighted windows: **Window A sparse low-confidence** and **Window B dense low-confidence**. Zoom-in plots show token confidence patterns in each window, with local mean confidence annotated.
- **Panel c:** Workflow schematic for **Balanced Fine-Tuning (BFT)**. It contrasts token-level weighting for sparse low-confidence tokens in Group A with sample-level or trajectory-level weighting for dense low-confidence Group B, aiming to stabilize gradients and reduce overfitting.
- **Panel d:** Model pipeline diagram: an **LLM** plus **biomedical trajectory** undergoes **BFT** to produce **LLM-BFT**, which generates descriptions of biomedical entities and maps them through a text embedding model into an embedding space.

Main visible finding: low-confidence token regions are separated into sparse and dense patterns, with different token compositions, and the proposed BFT strategy weights them differently to improve biomedical entity description/embedding behavior.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2: Medical competence and biological process reasoning. a : Medical competence is measured across axis-wise (left) and theme-wise (right). b : Biological reasoning benchmark.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel quantitative plot figure with experiment results. Panel **a** shows grouped point/error-bar plots of **Score** across model sizes **14B, 32B, 70B**, split into **Axis** and **Theme** task categories. X-axis labels include biomedical/scientific concept categories such as dataset-related and semantic/theme categories. Legend compares methods: **Base**, **SFT**, **DFT**, **BFT-sample**, **BFT-token**, and **BFT**.

Panel **b** shows line plots of **Regent-1 Score** versus **Model Size** for benchmarks **MsigDB**, **NeST**, and **GeneOntology**, with separate rows/conditions and the same method legend. A green dashed horizontal reference line labeled **GeneAgent** is shown.

Main visible finding: **BFT variants, especially BFT/BFT-token in red/pink, generally improve scores over Base/SFT/DFT across model sizes and benchmarks, with larger models often scoring higher and approaching or exceeding the GeneAgent reference in some settings.**

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure comparing gene embedding/model methods.

Panel a: Three 2D scatter/UMAP-style plots labeled `scGPT`, `GenePT`, and `BFT`, showing gene categories as colored points. Legend includes gene biotypes such as protein_coding, lncRNA, miRNA, rRNA, pseudogene, IG_V_gene, TR_V_gene, snoRNA, snRNA, and others. The visible finding is that GenePT and BFT show more separated clusters by gene biotype than scGPT, where points appear more mixed.

Panel b: Bar charts of AUC performance for methods `scGPT`, `GenePT`, and `BFT`. Left chart is `Single gene input` with x-axis tasks including `TF range`, `Dosage sensitivity`, `Biased in male`, `Biased in female`, and `Bivalent in hPAs`. Right chart is `Multi gene input` with tasks `GDA` and `PPI`. BFT generally has the highest or near-highest AUC across several tasks.

Panel c: Bar charts of clustering performance. Left chart is `Clustering performance (phenotype)` with metrics `ARI`, `AMI`, and `ASW`; right chart is `Clustering performance (cell type)` with the same metrics. Methods compared are `PCA`, `scGPT`, `GenePT`, and `BFT`. GenePT/BFT appear stronger than PCA/scGPT on several clustering metrics, especially AMI for cell type.

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel bar plot comparing model performance across four cell lines: `hepg2`, `rpe1`, `jurkat`, and `k562`. Each panel has y-axis `Score` and x-axis categories `DES`, `PDS`, and `MAE`. Bars are grouped by legend entries `BFT`, `STATE-SE`, and `STATE-small`, with error bars shown.

Main visible finding: `PDS` scores are highest across all panels, generally around 0.6-0.7 with large error bars. `DES` scores are lower, varying by cell line and model, while `MAE` scores are near zero across all cell lines.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 6: Workflow for extracting biological embeddings from LLM-BFT. a : LLM-BFT generates profile texts for entities of interest (e.g., a specific gene). The gene profile text is encoded by OpenAI TEXT-EMBEDDING-ADA-002 (the same text encoder GenePT uses) to obtain gene embeddings, so that GenePT (GPT-4o + ada-002) and LLM-BFT (BFT-70B + ada-002) differ only in the LLM that produces the profile text. b : For a single-cell dataset, gene embeddings are weighted by gene expression values to generate cell embeddings.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture schematic with two labeled panels, **a** and **b**. Panel **a** shows an LLM-based gene text embedding pipeline: a user prompt (“Tell me about gene.”) is processed by **LLM-BFT**, producing an LLM response with gene name/function/interaction text; texts for gene x through gene y are converted via **Text to embedding** into a **gene embedding (N, 2048)** matrix. Panel **b** shows a cell-by-gene expression matrix for **M cells** and **N genes** multiplied by the **gene embedding (N, 2048)** matrix to produce a **cell embedding (M, 2048)** matrix. Main visible message: gene-level text embeddings are derived from LLM responses and combined with gene expression data to generate cell embeddings.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 7: UMAP visualization of the multi-gene input task. a : For GGI, the input embedding of the classifier is directly concatenated from the embeddings of two genes. b : For PPI, the input embedding of the classifier is directly concatenated from the embeddings of two proteins.

Multi-panel UMAP visualization comparing embeddings from scGPT, GenePT, and BFT. Panels are labeled **a** and **b**.

Panel **a** shows three UMAP scatter plots titled scGPT, GenePT, and BFT, with axes **UMAP1** and **UMAP2**. Points represent gene or protein pairs colored by binary interaction label **0** and **1**. The visible finding is that the models show different degrees of separation between interaction classes, with GenePT and BFT showing more visibly structured class regions than scGPT.

Panel **b** shows three UMAP scatter plots for protein pairs, again comparing scGPT, GenePT, and BFT. Points are colored by interaction type legend: **activation, binding, catalysis, expression, inhibition, ptmod, reaction**. The visible finding is that BFT forms more separated local clusters by interaction category, while scGPT and GenePT appear more centrally mixed.

Multi-panel UMAP scatter plot figure with two labeled rows/panels, **a** and **b**. Each row contains three UMAP plots with axes **UMAP1** and **UMAP2**, colored by **celltype**, **patient**, and **phenotype**.

Legends show cell types including BCell, EC, Fibroblast, MSC, Mastcell, MonoMaphDC, NK, Plasma, SMC1, SMC2, Tcell, and Unknown; patient IDs including affected and control samples; and phenotypes including **Ascending only**, **Ascending to descending**, **Ascending w/ root**, and **Control**.

The figure shows single-cell clustering structure and annotation across patients and phenotypes. Visibly, panel **a** has more separated clusters, while panel **b** shows broader, more continuous/overlapping UMAP distributions. SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel UMAP embedding comparison figure from a single-cell multi-omics integration experiment. The grid has 4 rows labeled `BFT`, `BBKNN`, `Harmony`, and `scMODAL`, and 3 columns colored by `modality`, `celltype`, and `donor`.

Each panel shows a 2D UMAP plot with axes `UMAP1` and `UMAP2`. Legends indicate modality labels `ADT` and `RNA`; cell types including `B`, `CD4 T`, `CD8 T`, `DC`, `Mono`, `NK`, `other`, and `other T`; and donors `P1` through `P8`.

The figure compares how different integration methods mix modalities and donors while preserving cell-type structure. Visibly, `scMODAL` and `BFT` show stronger overlap between ADT and RNA modalities than `BBKNN` or `Harmony`, while cell-type clusters remain distinguishable across methods.

A delta sentence captures the vector difference between a perturbed and control state ( ∆ E = E stimulated -E control). figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: C2S-Scale unifies transcriptomics and natural language for scalable single-cell analysis. A , The C2S-Scale corpus integrates over 50 million single-cell transcriptomes curated from the CELLxGENE and Human Cell Atlas repositories, linking transcriptomic profiles with rich cell, tissue, and donor-level metadata as well as scientific abstracts and papers. B , C2S-Scale expands upon the Cell2Sentence framework by increasing model capacity up to 27 billion parameters, building a multi-task training corpus of over 1 trillion tokens, and expanding task diversity to include multimodal and multicellular inputs. C , Transcriptomic profiles are transformed into 'cell sentences', ordered sequences of gene names ranked by expression level. This enables the direct application of pretrained LLMs without requiring architectural modifications. D , C2S-Scale is initialized from pre-trained LLM checkpoints. An initial training phase on cell sentences is followed by instruction fine-tuning for a variety of downstream tasks. E , This unified training regime enables broad downstream capabilities, ranging from standard cell annotation to complex tasks like perturbation prediction and biological question answering.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel schematic overview figure for a biomedical AI model/workflow, likely a cell-language foundation model.

Figure type: conceptual workflow/model architecture diagram with labeled panels A-E.

Visible panels and labels:
- A. Data Sources and Annotations: icons for single-cell data, cell clusters, tissue sections, paper abstracts, and donor metadata. Reported scale includes 800+ datasets, 170M+ single-cell and bulk samples, 100M+ annotations, 21M+ perturbations, and 1B+ tokens.
- B. Scaling Dimensions: four boxed concepts: Model Capacity, Dataset Size, Multimodality, and Context Diversity.
- C. Cell Sentence Representation: converts a gene expression matrix with cells and genes into “cell sentences” listing gene tokens.
- D. Model Training Procedure: three-stage training flow: natural language pre-training with a base LLM, continued training on cell sentences to create C2S-Scale, then instruction fine-tuning for downstream tasks.
- E. Downstream Tasks: examples include cell type annotation, cell generation, perturbation response prediction, cluster captioning, dataset interpretation, and question answering.

Biological/model quantity shown: scale and modality of single-cell datasets, gene-expression-derived token sequences, and model training/use cases.

Main visible finding/message: the figure presents a unified framework for training a language-model-based system on large-scale single-cell, perturbation, metadata, and text resources, enabling multiple downstream biological interpretation and generation tasks.

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel benchmark figure with quantitative results for single-cell foundation/model methods.

Panel A shows a matrix of task performance scores across models, including C2S, scGPT, Geneformer, scFoundation, Gemini-1.5, GPT-4o, linear classifier, PCA, scVI, and CellTypist. Columns include cell type annotation tasks, cell embedding tasks, and generative tasks. Blue circles encode performance from 0 to 1, yellow outlines mark best performers, and gray dots indicate incapable/N/A. Bar summaries on the right aggregate predictive, generative, and overall scores.

Panel B shows compute scaling laws as bubble plots with x-axis training compute in log10 PetaFLOP days and y-axis BERTScore or gene overlap metrics. Bubble size denotes model scale, and colors distinguish tasks.

Panel C shows out-of-distribution cell type annotation accuracy versus training compute, comparing foundation models and simpler baselines, with bubble size indicating parameter count and shading/legend distinguishing model type.

Panel D shows LoRA fine-tuning performance for 27B and 2B base models, plotting training compute versus cell type BERTScore and dataset interpretation BERTScore for different ranks.

Panel E shows sample efficiency scaling with training samples seen on the x-axis and BERTScore or expressed gene overlap on the y-axes.

Main visible finding: the C2S models, especially larger versions, achieve top or near-top performance across predictive, embedding, generative, OOD, compute-scaling, and sample-efficiency evaluations compared with other single-cell models and baselines.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3: C2S-Scale enables natural language interpretation across biological hierarchies, from single cells to entire datasets. A , Overview of different scales of biological data interpretation, from single cells to cluster and datasetlevel annotation. B , Single-cell annotation performance on a diverse immune cell atlas [21]. The correspondence between ground truth and predicted labels demonstrates accurate annotation at the single-cell level. C , Cell annotation performance of C2S-Scale versus foundation model and simple model baselines in an in-distribution versus out-ofdistribution setting. C2S-Scale exhibits the smallest performance degradation when transferring from in-distribution (ID) to out-of-distribution (OOD) immune cell contexts. D , Cluster captioning performance on unseen data clusters. Models are tasked with generating descriptive biological captions given multi-cell context, with quality measured by BioBERTScore. E-F , Dataset-level summarization performance. Models generate natural language abstracts for entire scRNA-seq experiments, evaluated on held-out cells from seen studies (E) and completely unseen studies (F). Error bars represent standard deviation across test set samples.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing evaluation of a model for single-cell / spatial biological interpretation.

Panels:
- **A**: Workflow schematic titled “Multi-scale biological interpretation.” UMAP-style embeddings are shown at three levels: **Single Cell**, **Cell Cluster**, and **Dataset / Tissue**, with example user-model dialogue boxes for cell type identification, cluster description, and dataset summary.
- **B**: Confusion matrix heatmap comparing **True Cell Types** vs **Predicted Cell Types**, with a prediction accuracy color scale from 0 to 1.
- **C**: Bar chart titled **ID vs OOD Evaluation Setup**, comparing model accuracy across methods under **In-distribution (ID)** and **Out-of-distribution (OOD)** settings. Methods include C2S-Scale-28M, scGPT, Geneformer, scFoundation, scVI, PCA, CellTypist, and Linear classifier. C2S-Scale-28M appears highest or among the highest in both ID and OOD.
- **D**: Bar chart for **Cluster Captioning**, y-axis labeled **BERTScore**, comparing multiple models. C2S-Scale-27B appears best among shown methods.
- **E**: Bar chart for **Dataset Interpretation (ID)** with y-axis **BERTScore**, comparing models; C2S-Scale variants, especially larger ones, score highest.
- **F**: Bar chart for **Dataset Interpretation (OOD)** with y-axis **BERTScore**, again showing C2S-Scale models among the strongest performers.

Main visible finding: C2S-Scale models appear to outperform or match competing single-cell foundation/model baselines across cell type prediction, cluster captioning, and dataset interpretation, including out-of-distribution evaluation.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 4: C2S-Scale can interpret multi-cellular spatial context and predict niche neighborhoods. A, We fine-tune C2S-Scale on a variety of single and multi-cellular spatial tasks designed to enable C2S-Scale to perform spatial reasoning, including identifying whether cells belong to the same neighborhood, generating spatial neighbors, and predicting the niche label of a cell or group of cells. A 'neighborhood' is defined to be cells within a fixed radius from a central cell. B, C2S outperforms Nicheformer, scGPT, and other models in spatial neighborhood prediction accuracy (* = P < 0.05, ** = P < 0.01; McNemar's test). Dashed line represents random baseline accuracy (0.51). C, We use publicly available gene interaction databases including BioGRID and CellPhoneDB to construct natural language interaction prompts about gene interactions. Integrating gene interactions from BioGRID and CellPhoneDB individually improves performance, and their combination provides the greatest improvement (Panel B). These results highlight the multi-task transfer learning potential of C2S-Scale for spatially-aware biological modeling.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel schematic and result figure for spatial cellular neighborhood modeling.

Panel A shows a cartoon spatial cell neighborhood: colored circular cells inside a dashed radius `r`, with four task schematics labeled `Task 1: Neighborhood Prediction`, `Task 2: Neighborhood Generation`, `Task 3: Niche label prediction`, and `Task 4: Same niche prediction`.

Panel B is a bar plot titled `Spatial Neighborhood Prediction`. The y-axis is `Spatial Prediction Accuracy`. Methods on the x-axis include `scGPT`, `Nicheformer`, `Linear Model`, `GPT4`, `C2S`, `C2S w/ CPDB`, `C2S w/ BIOGRID`, and `C2S w/ BioGRID & CPDB`. Bars increase toward the right, with the combined `C2S w/ BioGRID & CPDB` condition highest at about 0.71. Significance brackets with asterisks compare several methods.

Panel C illustrates model inputs: a gene expression matrix for cells versus genes, interaction databases labeled `CellPhoneDB, BioGRID`, and a text-style question asking which gene codes for proteins interacting with a protein encoded by `GeneA`, with answer `GeneB`.

Main visible finding: incorporating protein interaction databases, especially BioGRID plus CellPhoneDB, appears to improve spatial neighborhood prediction accuracy over baseline models.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 5: C2S-Scale demonstrates superior single-cell question answering performance compared to state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs. A, Example QA scenario based on scRNA-seq data. B, Empirical comparison of C2S-Scale and SOTA LLMs on single-cell QA tasks, highlighting C2S-Scale's advantage in domain-specific reasoning. Error bars represent standard deviation across test set QA samples. C, Overview of the GRPO framework, which further refines model performance by training on preference data.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure combining a workflow schematic, benchmark plot, and optimization diagram.

Panel A shows a biomedical question-answering example for single-cell RNA-seq interpretation. It includes a context about inhibitory neurons in the thalamus, a “scRNA-seq Data” cell sentence with gene names, a question asking whether the cell is an inhibitory neuron, and an answer citing GAD1 and GAD2 as evidence for GABA synthesis and inhibitory neuron identity.

Panel B is a bar plot with y-axis labeled “BioBERT Score” ranging roughly from 0.65 to 0.85. The x-axis compares methods including C2S-Scale 410M SFT, C2S-Scale 410M GRPO, C2S-Scale 1B SFT, C2S-Scale 1B GRPO, Llama-3.2 3B, Llama-3.1 8B, BioMistral 7B, Gemini 1.5 Flash, GPT-4o-mini, and GPT-4o. Blue C2S models score higher than gray baseline models, with C2S-Scale 1B GRPO visibly highest.

Panel C is a workflow schematic for “Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)” using a C2S model. It shows multiple generated responses r1, r2, r3 normalized into advantages A1, A2, A3 using a formula based on mean and standard deviation of rewards.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 6: C2S-Scale models outperform existing methods in predicting cellular responses to unseen perturbations. A, Overview of the C2S-Scale perturbation prediction framework, which supports diverse perturbation types including drugs, cytokines, and genetic knockouts, utilizing Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to prioritize the accurate reconstruction of key gene programs such as apoptosis or interferon response. B, UMAPs comparing predicted vs. ground-truth responses for unseen perturbations across four models. Rows show: (1) all combinatorial perturbations, (2) CD4 T cells under IFNγ , (3) B cells under the held-out IFNβ + IL-6 stimulation. C2S-Scale aligns closely with ground truth in all cases. C, Benchmark metrics show C2S-Scale outperforms scGen, CellOT, scGPT, CondOT, BioLord, and linear models across all evaluation criteria. D, GRPO improves over SFT on L1000 (apoptosis response) and cytokine stimulation (interferon response) tasks, with gains in Kendall's τ , Pearson's r , and scFID. E, Benchmarking on the SciPlex3 dataset for unseen small molecule perturbations. C2S-Scale outperforms ChemCPA, scGPT, and CondOT across scFID, MMD, and Wasserstein metrics, demonstrating the model's ability to leverage pathway information for out-of-distribution prediction.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing a computational model and benchmark results for single-cell perturbation response prediction.

Figure type: workflow schematic plus UMAP/scatter embeddings and bar plots.

Panels and labels:
- Panel A: workflow for a “C2S-Scale Perturbation Model,” taking control inputs such as single-cell data and bulk RNA, supporting drug/cytokine/genetic KO perturbations, generating predicted responses, and evaluating against ground truth by gene-program similarity.
- Panel B: embedding plots comparing “Ground Truth,” “C2S,” “scGen,” “scGPT,” and “CellOT” across perturbation settings including unseen combinations, CD4 T cells IFNγ chronic, and B cells IFNβ + IL-6 chronic. Legend marks untreated ground truth in yellow and treated/generated cells in blue.
- Panel C: cytokine stimulation benchmark bar plots for scFID, MMD, and Wasserstein-2 distance, comparing C2S-scale 410M, C2S-scale 1B, scGen, CellOT, scGPT, ConDor, BioLord, and linear models.
- Panel D: cytokine stimulation response plots for IFN response and IL1000 apoptosis response, showing scFID, Kendall tau, and Pearson r for SFT vs GRPO at 410M and 1B model scales.
- Panel E: SciPlex benchmark bar plots for scFID, MMD, and Wasserstein-1, comparing C2S-scale 410M/1B against scGPT, chemCPA, and ConDor.

Main visible finding: C2S-scale models, especially the 1B version, show lower distributional error metrics than comparison methods in several benchmarks, while reinforcement learning/GRPO appears to improve correlation metrics over SFT in panel D.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 7: Virtual screening with C2S-Scale nominates a context-dependent modulator of antigen presentation. A, Schematic of the dual-context virtual screening workflow. The model predicts perturbation outcomes on MHC-I antigen presentation gene sets using initial states derived from primary tumor profiles (immune context-positive) and cell line profiles (immune context-neutral). B, Volcano plot displaying predicted drug effects in the primary tumor screen. Silmitasertib (red star) is identified as a high-scoring novel candidate. Inset details the top-ranking compounds, stratified by prior evidence: known MHC-I modulators (dark blue), plausible candidates with pathway links (light blue), and novel hits (grey). C, Experimental validation of the positive control, trametinib. Dose-response assessment of HLA-A,B,C surface levels (Mean Fluorescence Intensity; MFI) in WAGA cells treated with indicated concentrations of trametinib in the absence (gray) or presence (blue) of IFNβ (2 U/ml). D, Predicted context specificity of silmitasertib, showing a significantly higher antigen presentation score in the primary tumor context compared to the cell line context. E, Experimental validation of the novel hit, silmitasertib. Dose-response assessment of MHC-I MFI (normalized to vehicle control) in WAGA cells treated with silmitasertib without (gray) or with (blue) low-dose IFNβ (2 U/ml). Error bars represent mean ± s.d. Significance calculated via two-way t-test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons; ∗ P < 0 . 05 , ∗ ∗ P < 0 . 01 , ∗ ∗ ∗ P < 0 . 001 , ∗ ∗ ∗ ∗ P < 0 . 0001 .
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel biomedical experimental figure showing a virtual drug-screening workflow and validation results.

Panel A is a schematic workflow labeled “Virtual Screening Workflow”: primary tumors with immune context-positive profiles and immune-neutral cell lines are screened against a compound library of 4000+ drugs using C2S, identifying hits that increase MHC-I antigen presentation gene set score versus compounds with no effect.

Panel B is a volcano/scatter plot titled “Primary Tumor Screen Results,” with x-axis “Predicted Antigen Presentation Score” and y-axis “-log10(p-value).” Points are categorized by legend as Reported, Plausible, Novel, and star-marked “Silmitasertib.” A zoomed inset highlights drugs including crizotinib, nutlin-3, GSK-126, trametinib, afatinib, paclitaxel, and silmitasertib, with “16 / 23 Reported or Plausible.”

Panel C is a bar plot for “Trametinib + IFNβ (Known Hit - Positive Control)” measuring “HLA ABC MFI” across trametinib concentrations in nM, comparing DMSO only versus DMSO + 5 U/ml IFNβ. HLA ABC MFI increases with treatment, especially with IFNβ.

Panel D is a bar plot titled “Silmitasertib Context Specificity,” showing predicted antigen presentation score higher in “Primary Tumor Context” than “WAGA Cell Line Context,” marked significant.

Panel E is a bar plot for “Silmitasertib + IFNβ (Novel Hit - C2S-predicted)” measuring “HLA ABC MFI” across silmitasertib concentrations in nM, comparing DMSO only versus DMSO + 2 U/ml IFNβ. The main visible finding is that silmitasertib with IFNβ strongly increases HLA ABC MFI relative to DMSO-only conditions.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 8: C2S allows for conversion from expression information into cell sentence format with minimal information loss. Using a linear model fitted between rank and original expression, cell sentences can be converted back to expression accurately.

Bar plot comparing total FLOPs used by different models on a logarithmic y-axis labeled “Total FLOPs.” The title is “Total FLOPs Used By Different models.” The x-axis lists models: C2S-Scale-27B, C2S-Scale-2B, C2S-Scale-1B, C2S-Scale-410M, scFoundation, scGPT, Geneformer, scVI, Linear Classifier, CellTypist, and PCA.

Each bar has a numeric FLOP label: C2S-Scale-27B is highest at 5.2e22, followed by C2S-Scale-2B at 3.2e21. IFNβ-treated bars are higher than DMSO-only bars, with silmitasertib dose groups showing modest increases and significance brackets.

B, UMAP showing the 10 most frequent cell types in the Dominguez immune dataset [20]. C, The scFID is significantly lower within cells of the same cell type than between different cell types (two sample t-test; 10 samples within cell types, 45 samples between cell types; P = 2 . 23 × 10 -4 ). vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing a proposed metric/workflow and experimental results for single-cell embedding comparison.

Panel A is a workflow diagram: input cell/image-like data passes through a foundation model to produce embedding distributions across embedding dimensions. The distributions are summarized by mean `μ` and covariance `Σ`, compared with Wasserstein distance, yielding `scFID`.

Panels B and E are UMAP scatter plots. B is labeled “Cell Type Clustering - UMAP” with axes `UMAP 1` and `UMAP 2`, colored by immune cell type labels. E is labeled “Leiden Clustering (res=0.5) - UMAP” with clusters 0-17 in the legend.

Panels C and F are boxplots comparing `scFID` values. C is “Cell Type - scFID Comparison” and F is “Leiden - scFID Comparison”; both compare `Inter` versus `Within`, with significance marked `***`. Inter-group scFID is visibly higher than within-group scFID.

Panels D and G are heatmaps labeled “Cell Type - scFID Matrix” and “Leiden - scFID Matrix”, respectively, with colorbars for scFID. Diagonal/self-comparisons are low, while some off-diagonal comparisons are higher.

Main visible finding: scFID separates within-group from between-group comparisons, with higher distances between different cell types or clusters than within the same group.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1.  P3GPT features a novel architecture enabling efficient omics-data training and multimodal extensions.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture schematic for a multimodal biomedical AI model. It shows model input combining instruction tokens, OMICs data, and annotation matrices; a modality mapper processing OMICs features; optional text data and knowledge graph data mapped into shared embeddings; then learnable embeddings and multimodal input passed into stacked transformer blocks.

Visible labels include OMICs modalities such as transcriptomics, epigenetics, and proteomics; components such as FF, B.Norm, ReLU, MHA, ALiBi, transformer blocks, and frozen weights. A novelty box claims integration of multimodal OMICs, knowledge graph, and text, plus a new tokenization method for OMICs data and language-model-style task solving. No quantitative experimental result or plot axes are shown.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture diagram for an AI-driven biomedical research system. It shows roles such as Data curator, Investigator, Lab technician, and Scholar interacting with datasets, a database, “Precious-3 GPT,” a robotics lab, and “Science42: DORA.” Green dashed arrows indicate data retrieval, hypothesis generation, lab validation requests, experimental data generation, academic text production, and pain-point discovery.

The database panel lists domains including species, omics, tissues, cell lines, compounds, diseases, and demographics; omics/modalities include DNAm, expression, proteomics, tabular omics, knowledge graph, and text. Source logos include TCGA, PubMed, LINCS, ARCHS4, GEO, PandaOmics, CCLE, GTEx, UK Biobank, and INDRA.

A research areas panel lists drug discovery, natural compound modeling, omics interpretation, and geroprotector discovery. The main visible message is an integrated loop where curated biomedical datasets train a GPT model, which proposes hypotheses, drives robotic experiments, and produces scientific text for further research iteration.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure with quantitative plots evaluating an age-prediction or gene-expression model, labeled panels A-F.

Panel A shows histograms of human age groups and mouse age groups, with counts in thousands on the y-axis and age bins on the x-axis. Sample sizes are shown: human N = 18,224 and mouse N = 23,024.

Panel B shows a bar plot of the top-20 tissue counts, with breast, prostate, lung, kidney, and liver among the most frequent tissues.

Panel C shows training and evaluation cross-entropy loss curves over steps, with both curves decreasing and stabilizing around 6.2.

Panel D shows boxplots of Jaccard similarity for upregulated and downregulated genes, comparing P3GPT, GPT4o, and random models. P3GPT appears higher than GPT4o and random, with significance markers.

Panel E compares predicted versus actual human age for Horvathv1 and P3GPT using density plots. P3GPT shows stronger alignment with the diagonal and higher reported correlation, R² = 0.90, than Horvathv1, R² = 0.54.

Panel F is a Pearson correlation heatmap among age-related predictors or clocks, including Horvathv1, Hannum, Lin, PhenoAge, DunedinPACE, DNAmGrimAge, and P3GPT-based. The P3GPT-based measure correlates most strongly with Horvathv1 among the displayed clocks.

Multi-panel scientific figure with experimental data and summary visualization.

Panel A: Scatter plot comparing `Actual age, years/lifespan` on the x-axis with `Predicted age, years/lifespan` on the y-axis. Points are colored by mammalian species and marked by tissue type, with a pink overall trendline. The visible finding is a positive relationship between actual normalized age and predicted normalized age across many tissues/species.

Panel B: Dose-response line plot labeled `XL-888`, showing `N total cells (relative to DMSO)` versus `Log10(M)`. Two conditions are plotted, `siNC` and `siβPIX`, with error bars. figure_candidates.caption: Figure 5. P3GPT uses a rigid prompt structure to formalize research settings and communicate with the user.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Two-panel workflow/model figure. Panel A shows a text-prompt style biomedical query with tagged fields such as `<drug> UNKNOWN`, species `m. musculus`, tissue `muscle`, datatype `expression`, up-regulated genes `ORM2 DEFB4B`, down-regulated genes `MUC5AC TBC1D3E MSMB`, and instruction `diff2cpd`; the output lists candidate drugs `metformin`, `semaglutide`, and `acarbose`.

Panel B diagrams a Precious3GPT workflow. The left box shows an input comparison between control age group `20-30 years` and case age group `70-80 years` using an `age2diff` instruction, producing up- and down-regulated gene lists. These gene lists are then passed into another Precious3GPT prompt with a `diff2compound` instruction to output a list of potential geroprotectors.

Main visible finding: the figure illustrates a model pipeline that converts age-associated gene expression differences into candidate anti-aging/geroprotective compounds.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture diagram for a multimodal biomedical transformer model. The figure shows model input composed of instruction tokens, OMICs features grouped as upregulated/downregulated/annotation matrices, plus OMICs data, text data, and knowledge graph data. A green “Modality Mapper (MM)” maps knowledge graph token embeddings from `[n × k]` to `[n × 256]`, with smaller MM modules for text and KG inputs.

The central panels show “Learnable embeddings” and “Multi-modal input” with stacked colored token blocks of dimension `×256`, including frozen and trainable indicators. The right side shows transformer blocks with ALiBi attention, MHA, normalization, feed-forward layers, and repeated block stacks labeled `×32`; one path is marked frozen weights and another trainable/frozen distinction with flame/snowflake icons.

A legend defines ALiBi, MHA, FF, and B.Norm. A “Novelty” list claims combined modalities: multimodal OMICs, knowledge graph, and text; a new OMICs tokenization method; language-model-style task solving; and a unique multiomics multispecies dataset. No quantitative plot axes or experimental results are shown; the main content is the proposed model architecture and multimodal input pipeline.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Bar plot/histogram panel labeled “A” showing the distribution of human age groups. The title reads “Human age groups” with “N = 18,224”. The x-axis is labeled “Age, years” with binned age ranges from 0-10 through 90-100, and the y-axis is labeled “Counts, k”. Light blue bars show counts per age bin. The highest counts are in middle-aged groups, roughly 40-65 years, with lower counts at the youngest and oldest age ranges.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Line plot panel labeled “C” showing cross-entropy loss versus training steps. The x-axis is “Steps, k” and the y-axis is “Cross-entropy loss.” A legend indicates two cohorts: Training in blue and Evaluation in orange. Both curves drop steeply at early steps and then gradually converge/plateau around ~6.2 loss by ~500k steps, with training and evaluation closely matched after the initial phase.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Box-and-strip plot panel labeled “D” showing Jaccard similarity for genes. The y-axis is “Jaccard similarity”; the x-axis groups genes into “Upregulated” and “Downregulated.” A legend compares three models: P3GPT in purple, GPT4o in salmon/red, and Random in green. Both gene groups show P3GPT with the highest Jaccard similarity, GPT4o intermediate, and Random lowest. Significance brackets with asterisks indicate statistically significant differences between model comparisons.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Two-panel density/contour scatter plot comparing predicted age versus actual age in years. Panel labels show “Horvathy1” and “P3GPT.” Both panels have x-axis “Actual age, years” and y-axis “Predicted age, years,” with dashed diagonal reference lines indicating perfect prediction. Color legends labeled “Counts” show point density.

The figure measures age prediction performance. Horvathy1 reports R² = 0.54, N = 2,206, while P3GPT reports R² = 0.90, N = 2,824. The visible finding is that P3GPT predictions align much more closely with actual age than Horvathy1, indicating substantially better age-prediction accuracy.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Heatmap/correlation matrix panel labeled “F” showing Pearson’s r values among biological age or epigenetic aging predictors: Horvathv1, Hannum, Lin, PhenoAge, DunedinPACE, DNAmGrimAge, and P3GPT-based. Both axes list the same predictors, with a blue-to-red legend for Pearson’s r from about 0.2 to 1.0. The diagonal is 1.00. Strong correlations are visible among Hannum, Lin, PhenoAge, and DNAmGrimAge, while DunedinPACE shows lower correlations with several clocks. P3GPT-based correlates strongly with Horvathv1 (0.81) but weakly to moderately with most others.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Figure type: workflow/model architecture schematic.

Visible panels/labels: Two Precious3GPT diagrams. Left panel shows “Age group (month) 20-60 years” and “Age group (year) 20-60 years” inputs feeding a “regulon-GPT transformer.” Right panel shows a model output pipeline with “Model output,” “UP-regulated genes: gene A, B, C,” “DOWN-regulated genes: X, Y, Z,” then predicted “UP-regulated genes: X, Y, Z” and “DOWN-regulated genes: A, B, C,” feeding an “scGPT/component transformer.”

Quantity shown: Gene regulation direction prediction, specifically up-regulated and down-regulated gene sets.

Main visible finding: The schematic illustrates Precious3GPT transforming age-related inputs and gene regulation lists into predicted opposite regulation gene sets through transformer-based modules.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: Token analysis, BFT, and applications. a : Semantic composition of low-confidence tokens inside Group A (sparse-low) and Group B (dense-low). b : 4096-token trace illustrating one sparse-low window (Group A) and one dense-low window (Group B). c : BFT applies token- and sample-level loss adjustments. d : BFT-generated biomedical profiles are encoded by a text embedding model for downstream representation tasks.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure combining plots, schematic workflows, and model architecture.

- **Panel a:** Bar chart of **token composition (%)** comparing **Group A sparse-low windows** and **Group B dense-low windows**. Categories include interchangeable expressions, common vocabulary, biomedical entities, and causal/reasoning chains. Group A appears enriched for interchangeable/common vocabulary tokens, while Group B appears enriched for biomedical entities and causal/reasoning chains.
- **Panel b:** Line/trace plot of **4096-token response confidence**, with highlighted windows: **Window A sparse low-confidence** and **Window B dense low-confidence**. Zoom-in plots show token confidence patterns in each window, with local mean confidence annotated.
- **Panel c:** Workflow schematic for **Balanced Fine-Tuning (BFT)**. It contrasts token-level weighting for sparse low-confidence tokens in Group A with sample-level or trajectory-level weighting for dense low-confidence Group B, aiming to stabilize gradients and reduce overfitting.
- **Panel d:** Model pipeline diagram: an **LLM** plus **biomedical trajectory** undergoes **BFT** to produce **LLM-BFT**, which generates descriptions of biomedical entities and maps them through a text embedding model into an embedding space.

Main visible finding: low-confidence token regions are separated into sparse and dense patterns, with different token compositions, and the proposed BFT strategy weights them differently to improve biomedical entity description/embedding behavior.

Legend includes gene biotypes such as protein_coding, lncRNA, miRNA, rRNA, pseudogene, IG_V_gene, TR_V_gene, snoRNA, snRNA, and others. figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: Token analysis, BFT, and applications. a : Semantic composition of low-confidence tokens inside Group A (sparse-low) and Group B (dense-low). b : 4096-token trace illustrating one sparse-low window (Group A) and one dense-low window (Group B). c : BFT applies token- and sample-level loss adjustments. d : BFT-generated biomedical profiles are encoded by a text embedding model for downstream representation tasks.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure combining plots, schematic workflows, and model architecture.

- **Panel a:** Bar chart of **token composition (%)** comparing **Group A sparse-low windows** and **Group B dense-low windows**. Categories include interchangeable expressions, common vocabulary, biomedical entities, and causal/reasoning chains. Group A appears enriched for interchangeable/common vocabulary tokens, while Group B appears enriched for biomedical entities and causal/reasoning chains.
- **Panel b:** Line/trace plot of **4096-token response confidence**, with highlighted windows: **Window A sparse low-confidence** and **Window B dense low-confidence**. Zoom-in plots show token confidence patterns in each window, with local mean confidence annotated.
- **Panel c:** Workflow schematic for **Balanced Fine-Tuning (BFT)**. It contrasts token-level weighting for sparse low-confidence tokens in Group A with sample-level or trajectory-level weighting for dense low-confidence Group B, aiming to stabilize gradients and reduce overfitting.
- **Panel d:** Model pipeline diagram: an **LLM** plus **biomedical trajectory** undergoes **BFT** to produce **LLM-BFT**, which generates descriptions of biomedical entities and maps them through a text embedding model into an embedding space.

Main visible finding: low-confidence token regions are separated into sparse and dense patterns, with different token compositions, and the proposed BFT strategy weights them differently to improve biomedical entity description/embedding behavior.

figure_candidates.caption: Fig. 1 (A) The schematic overview of the OKR-CELL method. (B) The illustration of several downstream tasks implemented via OKR-CELL, including cell clustering, batch affect correlation, cell-type annotation and cross-modal retrieval.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel workflow/model architecture figure labeled **A** and **B**. Panel **A** shows a cross-modal cell-text pretraining pipeline: scRNA-seq/cell omics data and cell description text are tokenized, passed through **Cell Encoder** and **Text Encoder**, aligned by **cross-modal similarity**, and trained with intra-modal cellular generative pretraining plus cross-modal cell-text pretraining. It also includes a retrieval-augmented LLM workflow with **Retriever**, **Database**, **LLM**, and **Reliability Screen** for generating cell type definitions.

Panel **B** shows downstream application of a **pretrained cell encoder** from scRNA-seq/gene expression tokens. Outputs are shown as small UMAP-like embeddings and task panels labeled **Clustering**, **Batch-effect Correction**, **Cell Type Annotation**, **Zero-shot Annotation**, **Few-shot Annotation**, and **Cross-modal Retrieval**.

No conventional numeric axes are visible. The figure primarily depicts a multimodal single-cell foundation model workflow linking gene expression profiles with text descriptions for cell representation learning, annotation, retrieval, and downstream analysis.

(B) Bar plot of AvgBIO scores across four datasets (blood, kidney, hPancreas and hpbmc). (C) T-SNE plots of cell embeddings generated by different methods on blood and hPancreas datasets. (D) Bar plot of AvgBIO and AvgBatch scores of batch effect correction by different methods on hPancreas dataset. (E) Bar plot of AvgBIO and AvgBatch scores of batch effect correction by different methods on hpbmc reference dataset. SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel benchmarking figure comparing single-cell foundation/model methods across datasets.

Panels:
- **A**: Bubble/table-style summary for datasets **Blood**, **Kidney**, and **Hpancreas**, with metrics **ARI** and **AMI** across methods **Geneformer**, **scBERT**, **scFoundation**, **scGPT**, and **OKR-CELL**. Larger/darker bubbles indicate higher values; OKR-CELL appears highest in most rows.
- **B**: Bar chart labeled **AvgBIO**, comparing methods across **blood**, **kidney**, **hpancreas**, and **hpbmc**. OKR-CELL generally has the tallest bars.
- **C**: UMAP/t-SNE-like embedding panels for **blood** and **hpancreas**, shown for each method, with colored cell clusters.
- **D** and **E**: Bar charts for **AvgBIO** and **AvgBatch**, again comparing the same methods; OKR-CELL is visibly among the top performers.
- **F**: Radar/spider plot comparing metrics including **Isolated labels**, **KMeans NMI**, **KMeans ARI**, **Silhouette label**, **cLISI**, **Silhouette batch**, **Graph connectivity**, and **PCR comparison**. OKR-CELL has the largest overall polygon in several biological clustering metrics.

Main visible finding: **OKR-CELL** appears to outperform or match competing methods across clustering agreement and biological conservation metrics while maintaining competitive batch-related scores.

(C) Bar plot of accuracy and f1-score for cell type annotation by different methods on small-intestine, spleen and hpbmc reference datasets. (D) Bar plot of accuracy and f1-score for few-shot cell type annotation different methods on zheng68k and Great-Apes reference datasets. Multi-panel benchmarking figure for cell-type annotation across tissues/datasets.

Figure type: UMAP/scatter embeddings, confusion matrices, bar plots, and Sankey/alluvial classification maps.

Visible panels:
- **A**: UMAP-style cell embeddings for **eye**, **hPBMC**, and **small_intestine**, comparing models including **Geneformer**, **scBERT**, **scFoundation**, **scGPT**, and **OKR-CELL**. Each plot is colored by **cell type**, with legends listing tissue-specific cell populations. Titles report **AvgBIO** scores.
- **B**: Confusion matrices for **Kidney** and **Small intestine**, comparing predicted vs. true cell-type labels.
- **C**: Bar plots of **Accuracy** and **F1-score** across datasets including **small_intestine**, **spleen**, and **hPBMC**, comparing multiple models.
- **D**: Bar plots comparing **zero-shot** and related settings for accuracy across methods including **LangCell**, **scCUPNET**, and **OKR-CELL**.
- **E**: Additional accuracy and F1-score bar plots comparing selected methods.
- **F**: Sankey/alluvial diagrams labeled **Zero-shot Classification**, showing mappings between predicted and reference cell-type labels for **LangCell** and **OKR-CELL**.

Main visible finding: **OKR-CELL generally shows stronger cell-type separation and higher accuracy/F1 bars than the compared foundation models and baseline methods**, especially in zero-shot or cross-dataset classification settings.

(C) Bar plot of zero-shot cell type annotation performance by scCLIP-GPT(noisy) and OKR-CELL(noisy) along with original scCLIPGPT and OKR-CELL.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel experimental results figure with plots comparing `scCLIP-GPT` and `OKR-CELL`, including noisy variants.

Panel A: three line charts for `small-intestine`, `spleen`, and `hPBMC`, plotting performance versus `Gene Dropout Rate (%)` from 10% to 50%. The y-axis shows numeric scores. `OKR-CELL` generally remains higher and degrades less than `scCLIP-GPT`, especially at higher dropout rates.

Panel B: horizontal bar charts for `Accuracy` and `F1-score` across tissues/cell datasets: `colon`, `hPBMC`, `kidney`, `small_intestine`, and `spleen`. Legend compares `scCLIP-GPT(noisy)`, `OKR-CELL(noisy)`, `scCLIP-GPT`, and `OKR-CELL`. `OKR-CELL` appears strongest in most accuracy comparisons and many F1-score comparisons, while colon F1-score is low overall.

Panel C: grouped bar charts for `Accuracy` and `F1-score` across labels/datasets `great apas`, `eye`, `colon`, and `spleen`. The same four-method legend is used. `OKR-CELL` and its noisy version generally show higher bars than `scCLIP-GPT`, with strongest performance visible for `eye`.

figure_candidates.caption: Fig. 5 (A) Bar plot of bidirectional cross-modal retrieval performance (R@1,5,10) by different methods on our proposed SCxGEN-CT5K dataset. (B) T-SNE visualization plots of cell embeddings and textual embeddings of their corresponding cell types generated by different methods on eye and Great Apes reference datasets colored by ground-truth cell types. (C) Results visualization of cell based text retrieval on SCxGEN-CT5K dataset. The ground-truth and non ground-truth descriptions are marked in green and red, respectively. Note that, in addition to the original cell's paired cell-type textual description, any text descriptions corresponding to other subtypes under the same parent cell type are also marked in green. Samples with correct broad-type but incorrect subtype are considered partially correct and are highlighted in purple.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel experimental results figure comparing biomedical cell-text retrieval models: LangCell, scCLIP-GPT, and OKR-Cell.

Panel A shows bar plots for cell-to-text retrieval and text-to-cell retrieval, reporting R@1, R@5, and R@10. OKR-Cell appears highest across most metrics, especially R@10, with error bars shown.

Panel B shows UMAP/t-SNE-like embeddings for Eye and Grand Atlas datasets, with separate plots for LangCell, scCLIP-GPT, and OKR-Cell. Points are colored by cell type, and markers indicate modalities such as cell, text query, and generated cell ontology terms. OKR-Cell appears to align text/cell query markers more closely with relevant cell-type clusters.

Panel C is a table-like qualitative comparison using query-cell microscopy images and ranked text outputs from scCLIP-GPT, LangCell, and OKR-Cell. Retrieved cell descriptions are color-coded, with OKR-Cell generally showing more biologically specific matches such as goblet cell and kidney resident macrophage descriptions.

figure_candidates.caption: Table 1 Ablation studies for cell type annotation task on hpbmc and spleen datasets. The ✓ and ✗ denote the component is included or excluded, respectively.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Table-like experimental results figure showing ablation results for two datasets, `hpbmc` and `spleen`. Columns compare cross-modal pre-training data (`Original Text`, `LLM Enriched Text`), cross-modal pre-training objectives (`Info-NCE`, `PSW`, `CMMB`, `CCA`), and evaluation metrics (`Accuracy`, `F1-score`). Checkmarks and crosses indicate which data/objective components are included.

Main visible finding: for `hpbmc`, the best accuracy is `0.976` using both original and LLM-enriched text with `PSW`, `CMMB`, and `CCA`; best F1-score appears as `0.960` in another configuration. For `spleen`, the best accuracy is `0.780`, while the best F1-score is `0.765`, again associated with configurations using multiple objectives.

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel data visualization with three labeled panels: A, B, and C.

Panel A is a pie chart titled “Tissue Source Distribution,” showing tissue categories. The largest slices are Brain and Blood, followed by smaller categories including Others, Breast, Lung, Eye, Heart, Intestine, and a bracketed group of low-frequency tissues such as Kidney, Skin, Airway, Placenta, Bone Marrow, Liver, Lymph Node, and Adrenal Gland.

Panel B is a pie chart showing age or developmental group distribution. Labels include Adult, Middle Aged, Fetus/Embryo, Elderly, Young Adult, Other, and Child/Adolescent. Adult and Middle Aged appear to be the largest groups.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: BIOREASON Architecture. Schematic representation of our novel multimodal framework that integrates a DNA foundation model with a Large Language Model.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture diagram for a genomics-language model system. It shows DNA sequences passed through a frozen Evo2-1B model, then a learnable linear projection aligning Evo2 embeddings to Qwen3 dimensions. These projected DNA embeddings are stacked with tokenized text embeddings from a BioReason chat template and Qwen3 tokenizer, using special DNA pad/start/end tokens and a Qwen3 embedding matrix. The combined embeddings feed into a Qwen3-4B model.

Visible labels include “Stacked DNA and Text Embeddings,” “Frozen Evo2-1B,” “Learnable Linear Projection,” “Qwen3 Tokenizer,” “Qwen3 Embedding Matrix,” “BioReason Chat Template,” “Question,” and “Response (with reasoning).” The example biomedical prompt concerns chromosome 12, pathway definition involving LRRK2, CYCS, APAF1, CASP9, and CASP3, and asks about the biological effect of an LRRK2 allele. The response panel gives chain-of-thought-style tags and concludes “Parkinson’s disease.”

Main visible point: the figure illustrates a multimodal architecture combining DNA sequence embeddings with biomedical text prompts to generate disease-related reasoning responses.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2: BIOREASON Dataset Curation and Composition. A. Representative example of a KEGG Variant Network element from the 298 networks utilized in our study, illustrating the relationship between genomic variants and their corresponding disease annotation that serves as ground truth for generating mechanistic reasoning traces. B. Exemplar of a structured question-answer pair with an accompanying multi-step reasoning trace demonstrating the expected logical progression from genomic variant to phenotypic outcome. C. Pipeline for data acquisition, integration, and curation across the three BIOREASON tasks. D. Distribution of train/test splits across the three curated datasets. 10% of train dataset was used for validation. E. Distribution of disease categories represented within the datasets, highlighting the diversity of variants and diseases represented in the datasets.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific workflow and dataset summary figure for a biomedical question-answering/reasoning dataset built from KEGG variant networks and disease annotations.

Panels:
- **A**: Schematic of a KEGG variant network-to-disease example. Shows pathway, gene names, associated disease, and a ground-truth literature statement. Example involves **LRRK2**, pathway **LRRK2 -> CYCS -> APAF1 -> CASP9 -> CASP3**, and **Parkinson’s Disease**.
- **B**: Example question-answer pair and reasoning trace. The question includes a variant sequence and chromosome number, network definition, genes, and asks for the biological effect/disease. The reasoning trace identifies a **C-to-G substitution**, links it to an LRRK2 gain-of-function mutation, and concludes **Parkinson’s Disease**.
- **C**: Workflow diagram showing three task pipelines: KEGG pathway, coding variants, and coding non-SNVs. Data sources include KEGG, ClinVar, dbSNP, OMIM, COSMIC, and GPT-4o formatting. Outputs include **1,449 QA pairs**, **60,810 QA pairs**, and **36,088 QA pairs**.
- **D**: Stacked bar chart showing train/validation/test split percentages for KEGG, Task 2, and Task 3 QA pairs. Most data are train/validation, with smaller test sets labeled **290**, **1,233**, and **873**.
- **E**: Stacked bar chart showing disease-category composition across KEGG, Task 2, and Task 3. Legend includes benign, cardiovascular, immunological, metabolic, musculoskeletal, neurological, oncological, other, and sensory disorder categories.

Main visible finding: the figure presents construction of a variant-network biomedical reasoning QA benchmark, with thousands of generated QA pairs spanning multiple variant tasks and disease categories.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3: Case Study of BIOREASON's Output
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Three-panel schematic/table-style figure comparing a biomedical QA example across **Question**, **Ground Truth (KEGG)**, and **BioReason’s Output**.

Figure type: workflow/evaluation example for biomedical reasoning or question answering.

Visible labels/panels: left vertical label “KEGG Data Point”; panels titled “Question,” “Ground Truth (KEGG),” and “BioReason’s Output.”

Content shown: the question asks about chromosome 17, pathway “Actin,” genes including **PFN1/profilin 1**, and a **PFN1 allele**, asking for the biological effect and associated disease. The ground truth traces KEGG reasoning from a **C>T mutation in PFN1** to altered actin dynamics, axonal transport defects, motor neuron degeneration, and **Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)**. BioReason’s output gives similar reasoning and answers **amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)**.

Main visible finding: the model output matches the KEGG-derived ground truth that a PFN1 mutation is linked to ALS through disruption of profilin-1 function and actin cytoskeleton dynamics.

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture diagram. It shows DNA sequence, protein sequence, and natural language inputs passed through a unified BPE tokenization/encoder, then pre-training of a GPT-2 model labeled `GPT2-gene-eng`. The model is fine-tuned using PAWS English datasets and a sequence similarity classification dataset, producing `GPT2-gene-eng-ft`. Further fine-tuning branches use English summary datasets and English paragraph segmentation datasets, yielding models labeled `gene_eng_gpt2_para_seg` and `gene_eng_gpt2_summary`.

No axes or quantitative plots are present. The diagram depicts language capability transfer from English to DNA, with one branch marked “Verifiable” and a later genome-book application marked as “Unverified?” / “Indirect Verification?”. The visible main idea is a proposed pipeline for transferring natural-language modeling capabilities to genomic sequence tasks through unified tokenization and GPT-2 pretraining/fine-tuning.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2. Structure of gpt2-gene-eng . The model architecture is identical to that of GPT-2 small. Pretraining and instruction tuning use the same causal language header, the layer mapped 768 hidden units to 100000 units (the number of tokens in the vocabulary). Classication uses sequence classication header, The layer maps from 768 hidden units to only 2 units, where the 2 units represent the two classes id.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Model architecture diagram showing a GPT-style transformer. The left panel depicts tokenized text inputs passing through token embedding, positional embedding, dropout, and a 12× repeated transformer block with LayerNorm, masked multi-head attention, dropout, residual connections, feed-forward layer, final LayerNorm, and linear output layer. The right panels compare output heads: a causal language modeling head for pretraining with 768 hidden units to 50,257 vocabulary outputs, a sequence classification head for classification tuning with 768 to 2 outputs, and a causal language head for instruction tuning. Main visible point: the same GPT backbone can be paired with different task-specific heads for pretraining, classification, or instruction tuning.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3. On the left, Figure A shows the word vectors generated by the pre-trained model. Blue points represent DNA word vectors, and red points represent English word vectors. On the right, Figure B shows the word vectors generated by the ne-tuned model. Again, blue points represent DNA word vectors, and red points represent English word vectors.In Figure A, it is evident that the DNA word vectors and English word vectors are generally far apart, with a clear boundary between them. In contrast, in Figure B, the DNA word vectors and English word vectors are noticeably closer, with some overlapping regions. This further illustrates the reason for language capability transfer in the ne-tuned model.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Two-panel PCA scatter plot comparing DNA vectors and English word vectors. Both panels are titled “PCA of DNA and English Word Vectors” and plot Principal Component 1 vs Principal Component 2, with a legend showing DNA vectors in blue and English vectors in red.

Panel A is labeled “Pretrained model”: blue DNA vectors cluster on the left at negative PC1 values, while red English vectors form a largely separate cluster on the right at positive PC1 values, indicating strong separation between vector spaces.

Panel B is labeled “Finetune model”: the blue DNA vectors remain mostly on the left, while the red English vectors form a broader curved distribution extending from overlapping/nearby lower PC1 regions to high positive PC1 and PC2 values, suggesting altered geometry and partial proximity after finetuning.

routes.evidence_quote: We first evaluated unconditional generation under highly minimal conditions. In this setting, all explicit constraints were removed, and the model was provided only with a modality tag (Genomic DNA or RNA). It was then required to autoregressively generate the complete metadata fields, including species, gene name, and functional  annotation,  followed  by  the  corresponding  nucleotide  sequence.  For  generated mRNA sequences, we extracted the CDS regions and translated them into protein sequences, which were then aligned against existing databases using BLASTP 33 . We subsequently used Sentence-Transformers 34 to evaluate the semantic consistency between the model-generated functional annotations and the annotations associated with the top database hits. Sequence-logo analysis of these unconditionally generated mRNAs further recovered a Kozak-like translation-initiation context, which is a meaningful  local  sequence  grammar  (Supplementary Fig.  5).  The  results  showed  that  the  generated annotations remained well aligned with the corresponding generated sequences at the semantic level (Fig. 3b).

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing a genomics foundation model workflow and dataset/tokenization analyses.

Panels include: a workflow/model architecture schematic for a “GenNA Foundation Model” using genomic DNA/RNA data and transformer-based processing; a tokenization schematic converting multimodal input sequences into BPE token sequences and token IDs; several summary plots including pie charts, length-distribution histogram, donut chart of vocabulary token types, a bar chart of coverage versus k-mer length, and a scatter plot comparing token counts.

Visible quantities include genomic sequence/token vocabulary composition, sequence length distribution, taxonomic or data-source composition, k-mer coverage, and token-count correlation. Main visible finding: the tokenization/vocabulary appears dominated by a few major token classes, coverage decreases with increasing k-mer length, and token-count comparison shows a near-linear relationship.

figure_candidates.caption: Fig. 2: GenNA internalizes sequence-function mappings and evolutionary constraints
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure with experimental genomics/biomedical data. Panels are labeled a-j and include heatmaps, boxplots, contact-map-like triangular matrix, sequence-position effect maps, t-SNE embeddings, bar charts, and phylogenetic/tree diagrams.

Visible content:
- Panel a: Heatmap comparing protein levels across in-frame stop codons and paired codon substitutions, with a color scale.
- Panel b: Boxplot comparing RNA half-life change for “Watson” versus “Wobble” categories.
- Panel c: Triangular mRNA folding probability/contact-style matrix over transcript regions, labeled with 5′ UTR, CDS, and 3′ UTR.
- Panel d: Boxplots of attention ratio across gene regions, including promoter, tag, 5′ UTR, CDS, and 3′ UTR.
- Panel e: Horizontal boxplots showing change in protein levels for sequence/region perturbations such as CDS deletion, CDS ribosome-related features, and UTR mutations/deletions.
- Panel f: Heatmaps showing positional nucleotide effects across transcript sequence regions, including 5′ UTR, CDS, and 3′ UTR; one subpanel marks the start codon.
- Panel g: t-SNE plots colored by medication type and taxonomy group.
- Panel h: Horizontal bar chart of feature/category frequencies, with one highlighted red bar.
- Panel i: Heatmap relating therapeutic area and hosted species labels, with a percentage color scale.
- Panel j: Tree diagrams comparing transcript/protein length or taxonomic relationships.

Main visible finding: the figure summarizes learned or measured sequence-region effects on RNA/protein outcomes, showing that CDS and UTR features, codon changes, and organism/therapeutic categories are associated with measurable differences in protein level, RNA stability, attention allocation, and sequence-derived structure/features.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing a generative genomics/protein-sequence workflow and validation results.

Figure type: workflow schematic plus quantitative plots and sequence composition analyses.

Visible panels:
- **a**: Schematic of prompt-based sequence generation. Prompts include unconditional, species-specific, and downstream-task generation. Outputs show generated metadata and generated biological sequences with special tokens.
- **b, c**: Scatter plots comparing semantic similarity to model quality scores, with marginal histograms. Axes include semantic similarity and scores such as ZLAROR score and D-ASTI DI score. Reported Spearman correlations are around 0.32 and 0.43.
- **d**: Density plots comparing real genomes vs generated sequences for **CDS GC content (%)** and **CDS GC3 content (%)**.
- **e**: Boxplots of **CDS UC content (%)** and **CDS GC3 content (%)** across organisms including human, zebrafish, fruit fly, Arabidopsis, yeast, and maize. Stars mark real genome values.
- **f**: Circular/radar-like codon or amino-acid usage plots for the same organisms, comparing real vs generated distributions.
- **g**: Bar charts comparing frequency distributions between generated and real genomes across amino-acid/codon labels for multiple organisms.

Main visible finding: generated sequences broadly resemble real organism-specific genomic/protein composition patterns, including GC/GC3 content and codon/amino-acid usage, though agreement varies by species and metric.

figure_candidates.caption: Fig. 4: Controllable generation of structured non-coding RNAs and protein-coding sequences
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing evaluation of generated biological sequences, likely protein/RNA-related design results.

Panels include:
- **a**: Scatter/strip plot of **gRNA–siRNA score** or similar score versus categories including **Exact match**, **Wobble pairing**, **Isoacceptor**, and **Incorrect isotype**.
- **b**: Stacked bar chart showing **percentage (%)** of sequence-matching outcomes across amino acid labels, with legend categories such as **Exact match**, **Wobble pairing**, **Isoacceptor**, **Incorrect isotype**, and **No detection**.
- **c**: Histogram/density plot of **sequence length (%)** for **Class II** versus **Class I** tRNAs.
- **d**: Violin plots comparing **Real** and **Generated** distributions for internal bit scores at **5S, 5.8S, 18S, and 28S**.
- **e**: Scatter plots of **Iso-electric point (pI)** versus **Molecular Weight (kDa)** under several temperature/top-p conditions, colored by histone type.
- **f**: Boxplots of **ProtGPT2 perplexity** by histone type and generation condition.
- **g**: Protein structure/confidence-style diagram with labels for **N-term**, **C-term**, **intrinsic disordered regions**, and **globular domain**, colored by **pLDDT confidence**.
- **h**: Circular sequence/feature plots comparing natural and generated sequences under different temperature/top-p settings.

Main visible finding: generated sequences broadly resemble real biological sequence distributions across multiple metrics, though agreement varies by sequence class, matching category, and generation temperature/top-p setting.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing a genomics foundation-model workflow and tokenizer/data analyses.

Figure type: workflow/model architecture plus plots and tokenization schematic.

Panels/labels:
- **a**: Pipeline diagram for “Multi-Modal Nucleotide Sequences” into a “GenNA Foundation Model,” described as a Qwen3 decoder-only transformer with 3.6B parameters, trained using causal language modeling. Inputs include NCBI RefSeq genomes, genomic DNA/RNA, natural language annotations, XML tags, and a cross-modal BPE tokenizer.
- **b**: Pie chart showing dataset composition: RNA dominates over genomic DNA.
- **c**: Overlaid length distribution histogram/density for genomic DNA and RNA sequences, x-axis “Length (characters),” y-axis “Density.”
- **d**: Two taxonomic composition pie charts with categories such as plant, invertebrate, vertebrate mammalian, vertebrate other, fungi, and protozoa.
- **e**: Schematic of multimodal input tokenization from a biological sequence containing tRNA and nucleotide text into BPE tokens and token IDs.
- **f**: Donut chart of tokenizer vocabulary composition, center label “Vocabulary 6000,” with legend by token type/k-mer length.
- **g**: Bar chart of k-mer length coverage, y-axis “Coverage (Count / 4^k),” showing highest coverage for shorter k-mers and decreasing coverage for longer k-mers.
- **h**: Scatter plot comparing character count and token count with a fitted line, showing near-linear correlation.

Main visible finding: the figure presents a cross-modal nucleotide-language tokenizer and GenNA foundation-model pretraining framework, with RNA-heavy training data, broad taxonomic coverage, a 6000-token BPE vocabulary dominated by longer nucleotide tokens, and an approximately linear relationship between character count and token count.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing analyses of a sequence/gene language model using perplexity and attention metrics across genes, transcript regions, mutations, and species.

Panels include:
- **a**: Heatmap of perplexity on log scale comparing real gene symbols vs provided gene-symbol prompts, with matched prompts showing lower perplexity along the diagonal.
- **b**: Boxplot comparing perplexity for matched vs mismatched gene prompts; mismatched prompts have much higher perplexity.
- **c**: Attention matrix over token indices with labeled regions **5' UTR**, **CDS**, and **3' UTR**, showing strong structured attention within transcript regions.
- **d**: Boxplots of attention ratio while generating **5' UTR**, **CDS**, or **3' UTR**, with legend for attention on prompt, tag, 5' UTR, CDS, and 3' UTR.
- **e**: Horizontal boxplots of change in perplexity after mutation types, including CDS deletion, nonsense, stop-loss, missense, synonymous, and UTR substitutions/deletions; CDS-disruptive mutations show larger perplexity increases.
- **f**: Heatmaps of Δ perplexity by nucleotide position and mutated base, highlighting strong effects for deletions and around the start codon/CDS.
- **g**: t-SNE embeddings colored by molecule type and species, separating DNA/RNA and showing species-related structure.
- **h**: Bar chart of species-level perplexity, with lower values for some animals and higher values for yeast and Arabidopsis.
- **i**: Heatmap of Δ perplexity by true species label vs provided species prompt, showing lowest penalties on matching species.
- **j**: Two phylogenetic/tree diagrams comparing a tree based on perplexity penalty with a ground-truth tree.

Main visible finding: the model appears sensitive to correct gene and species prompts, transcript-region structure, mutation severity, and evolutionary relationships, with biologically disruptive CDS mutations and species mismatches increasing perplexity.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing a generative genomics/protein-sequence model workflow and quantitative validation plots.

Panel a is a schematic workflow with prompts producing generated metadata and generated nucleotide/protein sequence tokens for unconditional, species-specific, and downstream-task generation. Panels b and c are scatter/density plots of semantic similarity versus BLAST bit score, with reported Spearman correlations and mean similarity. Panel d shows probability density distributions comparing real genome and generated sequences for CDS GC content and CDS GC3 content. Panel e shows boxplots of CDS GC content and CDS GC3 content across Human, Zebrafish, Fruit Fly, Arabidopsis, Yeast, and Maize, with generated distributions and real genome reference markers. Panel f shows polar/radar-style codon usage plots for the same organisms, comparing real and generated sequences. Panel g shows amino-acid frequency bar charts by organism, comparing generated sequences with real genome frequencies.

Main visible finding: generated sequences broadly resemble real organism-specific genomic/protein properties, including semantic/BLAST similarity, GC/GC3 content trends, codon usage, and amino-acid frequency distributions, though some generated distributions appear shifted relative to real genomes.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure with experimental/model evaluation plots for biological sequence generation and classification.

Panels include:

- **a**: Violin/strip plots of **tRNAscan-SE score (bits)** across predicted tRNA categories: exact match, wobble pairing, isoacceptor, and incorrect isotype. Exact and wobble matches appear higher-scoring than incorrect isotypes.
- **b**: Stacked bar chart showing **percentage (%)** of tRNA detection outcomes by amino acid/isotype labels such as Gln, Trp, Met, Lys, Glu, Ile, Leu, Asn, Arg, Ala, Val, Thr, Gly, Pro, Ser, Asp, Cys, His, Tyr, Phe. Legend includes exact match, wobble pairing, isoacceptor, incorrect isotype, and no detection. Exact match dominates most categories, with more wobble/incorrect/no-detection fractions in some later categories.
- **c**: Histogram/density plot of **sequence length (nt)** comparing Class II tRNAs, labeled **Leu/Ser**, against Class I others. Class II sequences cluster around longer lengths near ~81-83 nt, while Class I clusters near ~72-75 nt.
- **d**: Violin plots comparing **real vs generated** ribosomal RNA internal bit scores for **5S, 5.8S, 18S, and 28S**. Generated distributions are visually close to real for some classes but differ in spread and central tendency, especially for 5.8S and large rRNAs.
- **e**: Scatter plots of histone protein sequences showing **isoelectric point (pI)** vs **molecular weight (kDa)** for natural sequences and generated sequences under different temperature/top-p sampling settings. Points are colored by histone type: H1, H2A, H2B, H3, H4. Higher temperature settings show broader generated distributions.
- **f**: Boxplots of **ProtGen2 perplexity** across histone types and generation settings, compared with natural sequences. H1 has visibly higher and more variable perplexity than core histones.
- **g**: Protein structure/cartoon-style biological diagram annotated with **N-term**, **C-term**, **intrinsic disordered regions**, and **globular domain**, colored by **pLDDT confidence** scale from 40 to 100.
- **h**: Four polar/radar-like codon usage plots comparing natural sequence patterns to generated sequences under different temperature/top-p settings.

Main visible finding: generated biological sequences are evaluated across tRNA, rRNA, and histone-like protein properties; many generated outputs resemble real biological distributions, while sampling temperature/top-p affects diversity, perplexity, and property spread.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: Token analysis, BFT, and applications. a : Semantic composition of low-confidence tokens inside Group A (sparse-low) and Group B (dense-low). b : 4096-token trace illustrating one sparse-low window (Group A) and one dense-low window (Group B). c : BFT applies token- and sample-level loss adjustments. d : BFT-generated biomedical profiles are encoded by a text embedding model for downstream representation tasks.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure combining plots, schematic workflows, and model architecture.

- **Panel a:** Bar chart of **token composition (%)** comparing **Group A sparse-low windows** and **Group B dense-low windows**. Categories include interchangeable expressions, common vocabulary, biomedical entities, and causal/reasoning chains. Group A appears enriched for interchangeable/common vocabulary tokens, while Group B appears enriched for biomedical entities and causal/reasoning chains.
- **Panel b:** Line/trace plot of **4096-token response confidence**, with highlighted windows: **Window A sparse low-confidence** and **Window B dense low-confidence**. Zoom-in plots show token confidence patterns in each window, with local mean confidence annotated.
- **Panel c:** Workflow schematic for **Balanced Fine-Tuning (BFT)**. It contrasts token-level weighting for sparse low-confidence tokens in Group A with sample-level or trajectory-level weighting for dense low-confidence Group B, aiming to stabilize gradients and reduce overfitting.
- **Panel d:** Model pipeline diagram: an **LLM** plus **biomedical trajectory** undergoes **BFT** to produce **LLM-BFT**, which generates descriptions of biomedical entities and maps them through a text embedding model into an embedding space.

Main visible finding: low-confidence token regions are separated into sparse and dense patterns, with different token compositions, and the proposed BFT strategy weights them differently to improve biomedical entity description/embedding behavior.

Multi-panel scientific figure comparing gene embedding/model methods.

Panel a: Three 2D scatter/UMAP-style plots labeled `scGPT`, `GenePT`, and `BFT`, showing gene categories as colored points. Legend includes gene biotypes such as protein_coding, lncRNA, miRNA, rRNA, pseudogene, IG_V_gene, TR_V_gene, snoRNA, snRNA, and others. The visible finding is that GenePT and BFT show more separated clusters by gene biotype than scGPT, where points appear more mixed.

Panel b: Bar charts of AUC performance for methods `scGPT`, `GenePT`, and `BFT`. Left chart is `Single gene input` with x-axis tasks including `TF range`, `Dosage sensitivity`, `Biased in male`, `Biased in female`, and `Bivalent in hPAs`. Left chart is `Clustering performance (phenotype)` with metrics `ARI`, `AMI`, and `ASW`; right chart is `Clustering performance (cell type)` with the same metrics. Methods compared are `PCA`, `scGPT`, `GenePT`, and `BFT`. GenePT/BFT appear stronger than PCA/scGPT on several clustering metrics, especially AMI for cell type.
