figure_candidates.caption: Figure 6: Workflow for extracting biological embeddings from LLM-BFT. a : LLM-BFT generates profile texts for entities of interest (e.g., a specific gene). The gene profile text is encoded by OpenAI TEXT-EMBEDDING-ADA-002 (the same text encoder GenePT uses) to obtain gene embeddings, so that GenePT (GPT-4o + ada-002) and LLM-BFT (BFT-70B + ada-002) differ only in the LLM that produces the profile text. b : For a single-cell dataset, gene embeddings are weighted by gene expression values to generate cell embeddings.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture schematic with two labeled panels, **a** and **b**. Panel **a** shows an LLM-based gene text embedding pipeline: a user prompt (“Tell me about gene.”) is processed by **LLM-BFT**, producing an LLM response with gene name/function/interaction text; texts for gene x through gene y are converted via **Text to embedding** into a **gene embedding (N, 2048)** matrix. Panel **b** shows a cell-by-gene expression matrix for **M cells** and **N genes** multiplied by the **gene embedding (N, 2048)** matrix to produce a **cell embedding (M, 2048)** matrix. Main visible message: gene-level text embeddings are derived from LLM responses and combined with gene expression data to generate cell embeddings.

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure combining plots, schematic workflows, and model architecture.

- **Panel a:** Bar chart of **token composition (%)** comparing **Group A sparse-low windows** and **Group B dense-low windows**. Categories include interchangeable expressions, common vocabulary, biomedical entities, and causal/reasoning chains. Group A appears enriched for interchangeable/common vocabulary tokens, while Group B appears enriched for biomedical entities and causal/reasoning chains.
- **Panel b:** Line/trace plot of **4096-token response confidence**, with highlighted windows: **Window A sparse low-confidence** and **Window B dense low-confidence**. Zoom-in plots show token confidence patterns in each window, with local mean confidence annotated.
- **Panel c:** Workflow schematic for **Balanced Fine-Tuning (BFT)**. It contrasts token-level weighting for sparse low-confidence tokens in Group A with sample-level or trajectory-level weighting for dense low-confidence Group B, aiming to stabilize gradients and reduce overfitting.
- **Panel d:** Model pipeline diagram: an **LLM** plus **biomedical trajectory** undergoes **BFT** to produce **LLM-BFT**, which generates descriptions of biomedical entities and maps them through a text embedding model into an embedding space.

Main visible finding: low-confidence token regions are separated into sparse and dense patterns, with different token compositions, and the proposed BFT strategy weights them differently to improve biomedical entity description/embedding behavior.

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel schematic/data overview figure from a biomedical paper. Panel `a` summarizes datasets used for an `H2O` foundation model workflow.

Figure type: dataset/workflow overview with a bar plot, anatomical silhouette, and downstream task dataset icons.

Visible labels and panels:
- Left: `H2O image FM data` with cylinder icons for `TCGA`, `GTEx`, and `In-house`, showing sample and patch counts.
- Center: `H2O ST FM and biomodal alignment data`, including a horizontal stacked bar chart by tissue/organ categories and a dataset label `HEST1K`; legend lists cancer/project abbreviations.
- Right: `Downstream analysis data` with task labels `Temporal`, `3D-Spatial`, and `Multi-omics`, linked to datasets `HTSA`, `OpenST`, and `HTAPP`.

Measured/shown quantities: numbers of samples, spots, and image patches across biomedical datasets; sample distribution across tissue/cancer types.

Main visible finding: the model is trained/aligned using large-scale histology/image and spatial transcriptomics-related datasets, then evaluated or applied to temporal, 3D-spatial, and multi-omics downstream analyses.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Figure type: workflow/model architecture panel for a spatial transcriptomics prediction model. It is labeled “b. Model Architecture and Training Procedure.”

Visible panels/labels: H&E imaging and spatial sequencing inputs feed into an Image FM and ST FM feature extraction pipeline. A contrastive learning block shows a similarity matrix, followed by “Conv & Concat,” a FiLM module, and “ST Prediction” output. A legend marks gray arrows as input, green arrows as output, flame icon as trainable, and snowflake icon as untrainable. Lower inset panels show Image FM finetuning from DINO V2 using TCGA, GTEx, and in-house data, and ST FM finetuning from a Single Cell FM using HEST1K.

Biological/model quantity shown: the model predicts spatial transcriptomics from histology-derived image features and spatial transcriptomics foundation-model features, with diameter feature extraction scales shown as 2 µm, 55 µm, and 150 µm.

Main visible finding/message: the panel presents a multimodal architecture where H&E image features and spatial sequencing features are contrastively aligned, combined through convolution/concatenation and FiLM conditioning, then used to generate spatial transcriptomics predictions.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel schematic/results overview labeled “c.” with title “H2O Results Analysis and Applications.” It shows six application panels: context-aware gene-expression prediction with a small heatmap labeled EPCAM, ACTA2, and n_genes; multi-modal informative clustering shown as colored point clusters; cell-cell communication shown as a network graph with highlighted nodes/edges; temporal continuity shown as a line plot with x-axis tick marks around 0.1-0.4 and y-axis values up to about 25; spatial contiguity shown as a 3D tissue/block rendering; and multi-omics integration comparing “Spatial Transcriptome” and “Spatial Proteome” image-like maps. The main message is that H2O supports multiple downstream spatial/single-cell analysis tasks, including prediction, clustering, communication inference, temporal/spatial structure, and multi-omics integration.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel biomedical results figure comparing spatial gene-expression prediction methods across datasets. Panels include boxplots of PCC for methods H2O, OmiCLIP, DeepPT, HistoGene, and BLEEP on ccRCC, PRAD, and IDCLymphNode; horizontal bar charts labeled “Best Gene Prediction Count”; a per-gene PCC comparison plot between H2O and the best competing result; a ranked “PCC Gap” gene plot; an enrichment-style bar chart with `-log10(P-value)` terms; and spatial expression heatmaps.

Measured quantity is mainly prediction performance using Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) and normalized gene expression across tissue spots. The visible finding is that H2O generally shows higher PCC distributions and the largest number of best-predicted genes across datasets, with spatial maps appearing closer to ground truth than competing methods for several marker genes.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel biomedical figure showing spatial transcriptomics / spatial domain and cell clustering results, t-SNE embeddings, and ligand-receptor interaction analyses.

Panels include:
- **a.** Spatial maps labeled **ST**, **Spatial Domain Recognition Image FM**, and **H2O**, with categorical color legends.
- **b.** Horizontal bar plots comparing methods, with H2O scoring higher than Image_FM, values around **0.66 vs 0.34** and **0.63 vs 0.44**.
- **c.** Cell clustering spatial maps for **ST**, **Image FM**, and **H2O**, with multiple cluster labels.
- A boxed **t-SNE map** section showing embeddings colored by clusters, alongside enlarged panels labeled **H2O Reproduced**, **H2O Newly Discovered**, and **H2O Regrouped**.
- **e.** Spatial ligand-receptor interaction/network visualization over tissue spots, including zoomed regions with arrows labeled **L: MIF, R: CD44** and **L: MIF, R: CD74**.
- **f.** Spatial component map and stacked bar chart of ligand-receptor counts, with legend listing many components and text box reporting **198 ligands**, **371 ligand/receptor genes**, and **1036 ligand receptors**.
- **g.** Bar plot of **Pattern Abundance (#)** for ligand-receptor patterns, with top terms involving **MIF-CD44** and related interactions.

Main visible finding: the H2O method appears to better reproduce and refine spatial domains/cell clusters than Image_FM, and identifies spatially organized ligand-receptor interaction patterns dominated by MIF-related pairs.

Workflow/model architecture schematic for a biomedical AI system labeled “Geneverse.” The figure shows preprocessing steps and training dataset construction from database descriptions, GPT-3.5 rephrasing, biomedical instructions, GPT-3.5-generated descriptions, and biomedical images. These inputs feed into a central multimodal/model training block with model logos/icons, then into downstream applications shown with biological icons, microscopy-like images, and check/cross marks.

No quantitative axes or plots are present. The main visible message is that Geneverse integrates gene/protein descriptions, GPT-3.5-augmented biomedical text, and biomedical images to support downstream biomedical applications.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2: UMAPs for the gene embeddings colored by gene functional information. Panels (a)-(c) represent the outputs of LLMs trained based on datasets from NCBI+GPT 3.5, NCBI only and GPT 3.5. We report the NMI score of each embeddings followed by their sources.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel UMAP/scatterplot figure with three panels labeled **a**, **b**, and **c**. Each panel shows colored point clusters in a 2D embedding with axes labeled **UMAP1** and **UMAP2** shown at left. Panel titles compare methods/settings: **NCBI+GPT 3.5 (0.377)**, **NCBI only (0.350)**, and **GPT 3.5 only (0.337)**. Points are colored by multiple categories, with a large central pink cluster and several smaller peripheral clusters in cyan, dark blue, brown, green, and maroon. The visible finding is that all three embeddings show broadly similar clustered structure, with the combined **NCBI+GPT 3.5** condition having the highest reported score among the three.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3: Results of sensitivity analysis for the training of different models. (a) The relation between the number of epochs and model performance of LLMs. (b) The relation between the number of cut-off length and model performance of LLMs. (c) The relation between the number of epochs and model performance of MLLMs for the protein task. (d) The relation between the number of epochs and model performance of MLLMs for the gene task. (e) The relation between the number of cut-off length and model performance of MLLMs for the protein task. (f) The relation between the number of cut-off length and model performance of MLLMs for the gene task.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel line plot figure with six panels labeled **a-f**. Each panel plots **Model performance** on the y-axis against either **Epochs** or **Cut-off length** on the x-axis. Legends show three metrics: **truthfulness** in red with star markers, **structure** in cyan, and **average** in blue.

Panels **a, c, d** vary epochs; panels **b, e, f** vary cut-off length values such as **512, 1024, 2048**. The visible trend is that **structure performance is generally highest and often near 1.0**, while **truthfulness varies more strongly**, especially increasing with cut-off length in panel **f** and remaining low in panels **c/e**. Average performance follows between the two metrics.

figure_candidates.caption: Extended Data Fig. 1: Definition of different evaluators or scorers. For the scorer focusing on truthfulness, we evaluate the matching level of model outputs for the description of gene properties and gene functions. For the scorer focusing on structural correctness, we evaluate the correctness of the structure of model outputs by comparing them to the limitations in the prompt. The logos of scorers are generated by DALLE (OpenAI, 2024).
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/scoring schematic. The panel is labeled “Scorer” and shows two grader components: “Grader for truthfulness” and “Grader for structural correctness.” Each takes a green input box labeled “The function of gene...” and points via arrows to evaluation outcomes.

It illustrates scoring criteria rather than experimental data: correct gene names/functions receive a high truthfulness score, wrong gene names/functions receive a low score; correct output format receives a high structural score, wrong output format receives a low score. No axes, quantitative plots, biological measurements, or experimental results are shown.

figure_candidates.caption: Extended Data Fig. 2: Figures of GOEA results. Each figure represents top 10 pathways in one cluster, and the pathways are ranked by -log(Adjusted P-value).
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific plot showing pathway/enrichment results as horizontal bar charts. Each panel is labeled by `-log(Adjusted P-value)` with panel indices `0` through `9`. The x-axes show `-log(Adjusted P-value)` values, and the y-axes list enriched biological processes/pathways.

Visible pathway labels include RNA polymerase II transcription regulation, phosphorylation, carbohydrate catabolic process, protein glycosylation, dephosphorylation, fatty acid beta-oxidation, glycolytic process, mitochondrial ATP synthesis coupled electron transport, and purine nucleotide biosynthetic/metabolic processes.

The main visible finding is that different clusters/panels are enriched for distinct biological processes, with strongest bars indicating the most statistically significant pathways in each panel.

Panel **a** includes a protein structure image and asks for the protein name; the LLM answer is “AF-O43280-F1.” Panel **b** includes a histology/microscopy image and asks whether gene **APOC1** is a marker gene of **macrophage** cell type; the LLM answer is “Yes.” The figure illustrates multimodal biomedical question-answering examples rather than quantitative experimental results.

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Bar plot comparing model performance by training dataset source. The x-axis is labeled “Sources of training datasets” with categories `NCBI`, `GPT 3.5`, and `NCBI+GPT 3.5`; the y-axis is labeled “Model performance” and ranges from 0.0 to 1.0. The legend shows three metrics: truthfulness, structure, and average. NCBI+GPT 3.5 reaches 1.0 for all three metrics, NCBI is near-perfect with structure at 1.0 and slightly lower truthfulness/average, while GPT 3.5 has lower truthfulness around 0.8, structure at 1.0, and average around 0.9.

figure_candidates.caption: Extended Data Fig. 7: Relation between top-k candidates and model performance.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Line plot showing `topk vs. Performance (LLM-RAG)`. The x-axis has top-k values `1`, `2`, and `5`; the y-axis ranges roughly from `0` to `0.9`. Three series are shown in the legend: `truthfulness` in blue, `structure` in orange, and `average` in gray.

Visible values trend downward as top-k increases. Structure is highest at topk=1 (~0.80) but drops to 0 at topk=5. Truthfulness is ~0.65 at topk=1 and 2, then decreases to ~0.32 at topk=5. The average declines from ~0.73 at topk=1 to ~0.16 at topk=5. Main finding: LLM-RAG performance appears best at topk=1 and worsens substantially by topk=5.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1. Longevity-LLM shows competitive performance in a range of Longevity Bench tasks. The tested tasks span the domains of transcriptomics, proteomics, and clinical record. Base Qwen-3 14B failed to produce valid outputs on all tasks.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel bar chart comparing model performance across biomedical prediction tasks. Panels include TCGA Survival (Binary), NHANES Mortality (Binary), NHANES Mortality (Pairwise), NHANES Mortality (Multiclass), GTEx Aging (Pairwise), Proteomic Aging (Pairwise), and NHANES Mortality (Regression).

Most panels use y-axis Accuracy, with a red dashed chance baseline; the regression panel uses MAE, months. Bars compare Qwen3-14B SFT in blue against Frontier LLMs in gray, with a legend at bottom right. The visible finding is that Qwen3-14B SFT is competitive with or near top-performing frontier LLMs in several tasks, leading in TCGA Survival and GTEx Aging, while gray models lead in some NHANES/proteomic tasks and lower MAE is better in the regression panel.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2. Longevity-LLM is a language model parsing the aging signal in DNAm profiles. (A) While SFT training on compiled datasets enables reliable age prediction, additional gains in performance can be achieved with RFT. Scatter plots show model performance in the holdout set of 1,438 DNAm samples.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel experimental result figure comparing age prediction methods. Panel A shows three scatter plots of predicted age versus true age in years for Horvath Clock, Qwen3-14B SFT, and Qwen3-14B RFT, each with a dashed diagonal reference line and reported metrics. Horvath: MAE 4.61, R² 0.895, p 0.946. SFT: MAE 5.91, R² 0.876, p 0.950. RFT: MAE 4.34, R² 0.914, p 0.950. Panel B is a bar chart of MAE in years comparing RFT, Horvath, and SFT, with RFT lowest at 4.34, Horvath 4.61, and SFT highest at 5.91; a significance bracket marks RFT versus Horvath. The main visible finding is that Qwen3-14B RFT gives the best age prediction performance among the shown methods.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3. Longevity-LLM captures age-dependent signal in proteomic data.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel performance comparison figure with plots and model benchmark results.

Panel A shows four scatter plots of predicted age versus true age in years, each with a dashed identity line. The models/conditions are labeled Kuo Mortality, Goeminne Chronological, Goeminne Mortality, and Qwen3-14B SFT. Points are colored by source, with a legend indicating Chia et al in pink and IoA in cyan. Each plot reports MAE, R², and p-value.

Panel B is a bar chart of MAE in years comparing Goeminne chronological, Goeminne mortality, Qwen3-14B SFT, and Kuo mortality. Qwen3-14B SFT has MAE 7.9, lower than Kuo mortality at 10.6 but higher than the two Goeminne models around 6.7-6.9.

Panel C is a horizontal bar chart of Jaccard Index across models. Qwen3-14B SFT has the highest visible Jaccard Index, 0.0718, followed by grok-3, grok-4, o3, and other LLMs. The main finding is that Qwen3-14B SFT performs competitively in age prediction and ranks highest in the Jaccard Index comparison.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Bar chart showing model performance on “NHANES Mortality (Multiclass)”. The y-axis ranges roughly from 0.15 to 0.45, with a dashed orange horizontal reference line at about 0.25. Multiple models are compared on the x-axis, including GPT-style and biomedical/clinical models. A dark blue highlighted bar labeled around 0.343 corresponds to a clinical model, while the highest gray bars reach about 0.389. The main visible finding is that several models outperform the dashed baseline, with the best models near 0.39 and the highlighted model in the mid-performing range.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scatter plot figure with four panels labeled under panel A. Each panel compares `True age, years` on the x-axis against `Predicted age, years` on the y-axis, with a dashed diagonal identity line. A legend in the first panel labels two data sources: pink points for `Chia et al` and cyan points for `IoA`.

Panels shown:
- `Kuo Mortality`: weak alignment between predicted and true age; inset reports MAE = 10.6, R² = 0.028, ρ = 0.800.
- `Goeminne Chronological`: points cluster close to the identity trend; MAE = 6.7, R² = 0.547, ρ = 0.937.
- `Goeminne Mortality`: moderate alignment; MAE = 6.9, R² = 0.554, ρ = 0.742.
- `Qwen3-14B SFT`: broader scatter with moderate association; MAE = 7.9, R² = 0.330, ρ = 0.713.

The figure appears to evaluate age prediction models or methods, showing that the Goeminne chronological/mortality models have visibly stronger prediction agreement than Kuo mortality, while Qwen3-14B SFT shows intermediate performance.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Bar plot panel labeled **B** showing **MAE, years** on the y-axis. Four model/condition bars are shown: **Goeminne (chrono)** 6.7, **Goeminne (mortality)** 6.9, **Qwen3-14B (SFT)** 7.9 highlighted in blue, and **Kuo (mortality)** 10.6. A red dashed horizontal line labeled **Group mean prediction** lies near 10.6 years.

Main visible finding: **Qwen3-14B (SFT)** has higher MAE than the two Goeminne baselines but lower MAE than the Kuo mortality model and the group mean prediction level.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Bar plot panel labeled “C” showing Jaccard Index on the x-axis for multiple language models on the y-axis. The top highlighted blue bar is “Qwen3-14B SFT” with Jaccard Index 0.0718. Other gray bars include grok-3 0.0298, grok-4 0.0224, o3 0.0205, gpt-5 0.0171, gpt-4.1 0.0156, gpt-5.2 0.0142, claude-sonnet-4-5 0.0117, gpt-4.1-mini 0.0113, o4-mini 0.0099, gemini-3-flash 0.0073, gpt-5-mini 0.0061, gemini-2.5-pro 0.0053, gemini-3-pro 0.0044, gemini-2.5-flash 0.0041, and DeepSeek-R1-0528 0.0040. Main finding: Qwen3-14B SFT has the highest Jaccard Index, substantially exceeding all compared models.

Radar/spider plot comparing multiple DNA foundation models across epigenomic/chromatin marks. The circular axes are labeled with histone modifications and chromatin features including H3K4ME1, H3K14AC, H3, H4AC, H4, H3K9AC, H3K79ME3, H3K4ME3, H3K4ME2, and H3K36ME3. figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3. (a) Cross Entropy Loss on test set during pretraining. The models with varying sizes show a stable decrease in loss. (b) No-Bias Normalization Layer stabilizes the average value of feed-forward weights in transformer layers. This pattern is consistent across all the transformer blocks.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Two-panel line plot showing language model training dynamics versus tokens seen.

Figure type: multi-line experimental result plot.

Panels and axes:
- Panel (a): CrossEntropyLoss versus Tokens Seen (billions).
- Panel (b): Avg Weight versus Tokens Seen (billions).
- X-axis ranges from 0 to 300 billion tokens.
- Legend compares model/data scale conditions: 20M, 60M, 116M, 300M, 700M, and 1B.

Measured quantities:
- Cross-entropy loss during training.
- Average weight metric over training tokens.

Main visible finding:
- Cross-entropy loss decreases over training for all curves, with larger-scale conditions generally achieving lower loss.
- In panel (b), the 20M curve shows much larger and noisier growth in average weight, while most larger models remain comparatively stable; the 60M curve trends downward below zero.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 4. Overview of of Omni-DNA architecture. In pretraining , Omni-DNA are trained on DNA only with next-token prediction. Multi-task finetuning enables the model to perform diverse tasks including classification, function prediction, and DNA-to-image.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture diagram for an “Omni-DNA (Auto-Regressive Transformer)” system. The figure has two main phases: “Pretraining” on the left and “Multi-task Finetuning” on the right. It shows next-token prediction with a BPE tokenizer over DNA-like tokens such as `TATA`, `GCGC`, and `G`, feeding token IDs into the transformer.

The finetuning side shows task-unified inputs with “Instructions” and “Response” tokens for multiple downstream tasks, including “Classification,” “Function Prediction,” and “DNA2Images.” Example prompts ask whether DNA is H3/H4, predict DNA function, and map DNA to handwritten digits. The diagram emphasizes a shared expanded BPE tokenizer and task unification format for DNA-to-label, DNA-to-text, and DNA-to-tensor outputs. No quantitative axes or experimental results are shown.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 5. F1 scores and invalid percentages for Needle-in-DNA , averaged and per class . Omni-DNA outperforms both baselines.
vlm_descriptions:

Below are bar charts of F1 Score and Invalid % for model comparisons. Legend: Omni-DNA, OLMO, Unpretrained, and a red dashed Random Guess baseline. Panels include Average, Class 0, Class 1, Class 2, and Class 3. The y-axes are “F1 Score ↑” and “Invalid % ↓”.

Main visible finding: Omni-DNA achieves near-perfect F1 scores across classes with low invalid output rates, while OLMO and especially the unpretrained model show lower F1 or higher invalid percentages in several classes.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 6. Losses for Omni-DNA (116M) pretrained with ALiBi and RoPE, indicating RoPE's faster convergence and lower losses.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Line plot of training/test cross entropy loss versus step `t`. The x-axis is labeled `t` and runs from 0 to about 800,000; the y-axis is labeled `Cross Entropy Loss (↓)` and spans roughly 4.0 to 5.75. The legend compares four curves/bands: Omni-DNA with Abilii test loss in orange, Omni-DNA with RoPE test loss in green, Abilii train loss in pink, and RoPE train loss in blue/purple. Both methods show a steep early loss drop followed by gradual decline; RoPE appears slightly lower than Abilii over much of training, especially later steps.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 7. Impact of model size on performance degradation due to vocabulary expansion. Larger models exhibit better resilience against distribution shifts.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Plot comparing model performance by parameter count. It shows F1 score on `Promoter-TATA` on the y-axis versus `Parameter Count` on the x-axis, with points at 20M, 60M, 116M, 300M, 700M, and 1B. Legend indicates orange circles for “Classification Head Approach” and green stars for “Predict Labels as New Token.” Vertical lines connect paired results, with percentage drops annotated.

Main visible finding: the classification-head approach consistently achieves higher F1 scores than predicting labels as new tokens, with the largest visible gap around 60M parameters and smaller gaps at larger model sizes.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 8. Impact of the token replication factor α on the promoter TATA classification task.
vlm_descriptions:

The x-axis is labeled “Repeating Factor” with values around 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12; the y-axis is labeled “F1-Score” ranging roughly from 0.4 to 0.9+. Two curves are shown: orange “Omni-DNA 116M” and green “Omni-DNA 1B.” Both improve as repeating factor increases. SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific schematic showing a genomic foundation model workflow and biological interpretation.

Panel A depicts the OmniNA model pipeline: pre-training on the NCBI nucleotide database using masked sequence annotation, data processing with prefix-style prompts, and large-scale transformer pre-training. It then shows fine-tuning on genomic tasks such as promoter prediction, mutation pathogenicity classification, and RNA off-target prediction. Labels include “Stage 1: Pre-training on NCBI nucleotide database,” “Stage 2: Fine-tuning for genomic tasks,” “The pre-trained OmniNA,” and “Downstream tasks.”

Panel B is a biological/genomic diagram illustrating chromatin and DNA-level functional genomics. It shows nucleosomes, histone occupation, transcription factor binding, chromosome accessibility, enhancer, promoter, splice site, poly(A) signal, translation initiation site, DNA methylation, and species differentiation across bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes.

Main visible finding/message: the figure presents a model architecture/workflow for learning from large-scale nucleotide sequences and applying the pretrained model to diverse genomic prediction and functional element characterization tasks.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing model evaluation and embedding analyses for nucleotide sequence classification.

Panels include:
- **A**: Table comparing models **OmniNA-1.7B, OmniNA-330M, OmniNA-66M, OmniNA-1.7B, OmniNA-330M, OmniNA-66M** across tasks: nucleotide sequence classification, taxonomy classification, and enzyme classification. Metrics shown are **precision, recall, F1**.
- **B**: Example nucleotide inputs with colored tokenization segments and response labels, comparing models such as **OmniNA-1.7B**, **OmniNA-330M**, and **OmniNA-66M**.
- **C, D**: Line plots for **taxonomy** and **gene function**, showing **token number** versus **token frequency**, plus summary token number values.
- **E, G**: Boxplots of **cosine similarity**, comparing OmniNA models against a randomized/control condition.
- **F**: t-SNE embedding plot with labeled biological categories such as **mRNA of dehydrogenase**, **mRNA of oxidase**, **chloroplast CDS/mRNA**, and **NLS complex subunit 2**.
- **H**: t-SNE embedding plot for **HIV1 genes** with a color legend, plus a gene-structure schematic and example model responses.

Main visible finding: OmniNA models appear to produce biologically meaningful tokenization and embedding structure, with higher cosine similarity and clustered t-SNE representations corresponding to gene or functional categories.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing learned token/sequence embeddings and biological classification results, mostly visualized with t-SNE plots. Panels are labeled A-J.

Figure type: dimensionality reduction plots, heatmap, conservation contours, taxonomy clustering, phylogenetic tree, distribution/statistical plot, and viral protein embedding plot.

Visible content:
- A-B: t-SNE token embedding plots with colored clusters and example tokens for gene names/functions, nucleotide sequences, riboviruses, duplodnaviria, and monodnaviria.
- C: Heatmap of feature representation across model layers, with ARI scale and marked best ARI.
- D: t-SNE sequence conservation map with contour-like trajectories colored high vs low conservation.
- E-F: t-SNE taxonomy/classification plots separating bacteria/virus/fungi and bacteria/archaea groups.
- G: Circular phylogenetic tree annotated with bacterial/archaeal taxa.
- H-I: SARS-CoV-2 phylogeny/variant embedding and pairwise cosine similarity distribution across clades, with significance markers.
- J: t-SNE plot of viral functional proteins, with legend for coding sequence, capsid, matrix, polymerase, nucleocapsid, virulence factor, envelope, hemagglutinin, neuraminidase, and spike proteins.

Main visible finding: learned representations appear to cluster biological tokens, sequences, taxa, viral variants, and protein functions in biologically meaningful groups, with separation by taxonomy, conservation, and viral functional categories.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel biomedical ML benchmark figure comparing OmniHelix model variants against benchmarks across genomic/biological prediction tasks. It contains radar plots, bar charts, dot/heatmap-style summaries, violin plots, and a scatter plot.

Visible panels include:
- A: Radar chart with regulatory element categories such as promoter, enhancer, insulator, silencer, active promoter/enhancer; legend compares OmniHelix-1.7B, OmniHelix-330M, OmniHelix-66M, OmniHelix-68M, and Benchmark.
- B-D: Bar plots of F1 scores for PAS/TIS, splice site, and gRNA off-target prediction.
- E: Dot plot across many tissues/cell types, showing recall/precision-style performance for chromatin accessibility.
- F: Table-like heatmap summarizing tasks including chromatin accessibility, histone, and transcription factor, with metrics F1/precision/recall across Benchmark, Enformer, Sei, Expecto, and OmniHelix sizes.
- G: Violin plot for pathogenicity of mutation with grouped distributions and significance markers.
- H: Radar plot for specific genes, comparing EVE and OmniHelix-1.7B.
- Bottom panels: Bar plots for pathogenic virus and taxonomic ranks such as family, class, order, phylum, plus a scatter plot comparing OmniHelix F1 score against benchmark F1 score.

Main visible finding: OmniHelix variants, especially OmniHelix-1.7B, generally show higher or competitive performance across many genomic prediction and pathogenicity-related benchmarks compared with baseline/benchmark methods.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel biomedical figure showing mutation-effect predictions and protein/domain-level visualizations. Panels include:

- **A:** Schematic of an “OmniHelix mutation effect score” for a genomic sequence around `chr7:1321843 A>G`, with formula comparing predicted mutation effects.
- **B:** Bar/line plots for mutation effect bins in **TIS** and **PAS**, showing proportions of benign vs pathogenic variants and increasing score trend.
- **C:** Line/bar comparison of **predicted mutation effect** versus **real mutation effect** across bases 1–23, with error bars.
- **D/E:** Heatmap-style mutation effect maps across **BRCA1 amino acid sequence**, annotated with domains including zinc finger, BRCT1, and BRCT2.
- **F:** Protein structure visualization of **BRCA1**, colored by mutation effect, highlighting zinc finger and BRCT regions.
- **G/H:** Similar domain and mutation-effect heatmap for **CHD7**, with annotated domains such as chromo 1–2, ATP-binding, helicase C-terminal, SANT, and BRK.
- **I:** Protein structure visualization of **CHD7**, highlighting chromo and ATP-binding regions.

Main visible finding: predicted mutation effects vary across sequence positions and protein domains, with stronger effects concentrated in known functional domains of BRCA1 and CHD7.

Panel a: Schematic overview of “ProCyon,” described as a unified latent space for proteins and phenotypes. It lists task categories such as protein function retrieval, domain-based protein retrieval, protein interaction prediction, disease-associated protein retrieval, and contextual target retrieval, with example prompts and outputs.

Panel b: Workflow/model architecture diagram. It shows user prompts for protein retrieval and phenotype generation, inputs such as disease text or protein sequence/structure, protein LM and text encoder modules, retrieval/augmented text generation, and example retrieved proteins or phenotype descriptions with scores.

Labels include Interaction, Function, Disease, Domain, and Therapeutics, with bars for items such as GO Function, GO Component, Reactome, UniProt, Enzyme Commission, DisGeNet, OMIM, Pfam, SMART, PROSITE, and drug/target-related sources. The radial axis is “Number of Samples,” ranging up to about 3,000,000.

Main visible finding: the figure presents ProCyon as a multimodal protein-phenotype model supporting retrieval, prediction, and generation tasks across protein function, interaction, disease, domain, and therapeutic datasets.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel biomedical AI evaluation figure showing ProCyon performance on protein-function and disease-association retrieval tasks.

Panels include:
- **a**: Workflow schematic. A user prompt asks for a cellular component and biological process; ProCyon outputs ranked proteins with percentile scores.
- **b**: Bar plots of **Retrieval Fmax** comparing models across tasks: protein function, cellular component, biological pathway, disease association, drug target, and drug-protein interaction. Models include Random, BLAST+kNN, ESM variants, GearNet, BioTranslator, ProtST, and ProCyon.
- **c**: Bar plots comparing ProCyon in-context splits: many-shot, few-shot, and zero-shot across the same task categories.
- **d**: Example protein **Q12948: FOXC1** connected to phenotype labels including heart development, regulation of HPSC differentiation, and regulation of mitotic cell cycle.
- **e**: Bar plot comparing ProCyon, phenotype prompt, and aggregated individual ranks for proteins with two, three, or four functions.
- **f**: Box/strip plots of percentile scores by evidence type: genetics, somatic mutation, animal model, molecular pathway, literature, and drug mechanism of action.
- **g**: Disease retrieval prompt example for **autism spectrum disorder**, with highlighted diagnostic features and supporting associated features; adjacent percentile distributions show retrieval ranking.
- **h**: UMAP-like embedding plot comparing prompt embeddings and protein embeddings, with labeled prompt specificity levels from “Basic phenomenon” to “Basic phenomenon, Mechanistic insights, Precise function,” and a marked protein **STING**.

Main visible finding: ProCyon generally achieves higher retrieval performance than baseline protein-language or graph models across functional, pathway, disease, and drug-related retrieval tasks, and more detailed prompts appear to improve percentile ranking.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3: PROCYON generates accurate responses and phenotype descriptions from multimodal prompts. a) In QA, PROCYON receives a multimodal prompt (protein + phenotype description) and outputs a yes/no answer. b) Benchmarking QA accuracy across models and knowledge domains. Error bars show bootstrapped 95% CIs. c) PROCYON's QA accuracy across different PROCYON-INSTRUCT splits. d) PROCYON tokenizes protein sequences and 3D structures using a multimodal encoder; LLMs must use text surrogates, many of which are not generalizable (gene symbol, UniProt ID). e) QA performance comparison between PROCYON and LLMs using HGNC gene symbols. f) In phenotype generation, PROCYON processes multimodal inputs (proteins, natural language, small molecules) to output open-ended phenotype descriptions. g) Phenotype generation benchmark using reference text similarity (mean BERTScore F 1 ). Hatching indicates ability to generalize to unseen proteins. h) Phenotype generation benchmark using LLM-based judging. Win rate refers to preference over PROCYON; models grouped by parameter count.

X-axis is **Accuracy**. Methods include BLAST-kNN, ESM2-kNN/MLP, ESM3-kNN/MLP, GearNet-kNN/MLP, ProtLLM, and ProCyon.
- **c**: Bar chart comparing ProCyon-Instruct split performance across many-shot, few-shot, and zero-shot settings for the same task categories. X-axis is **Accuracy**.

- **e**: Accuracy bar charts comparing Llama-HG, Mistral-HG, GPT4-HG, and ProCyon for Function, Pathway, and Disease.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 4: PROCYON models domains, peptides, and small molecules beyond proteins. a) PROCYON predicts the small molecule binding domain on proteins, where the input is the description and molecular structure of a drug, and the output is a ranked list of domains on a target protein. In this example, PROCYON retrieves domains of MGAM given the drug miglitol and correctly prioritizes the binding domain for miglitol as the first among the MGAM's nine domains. Each domain is identified by the Pfam ID and the index of the first amino acid in the domain. b) PROCYON ranks the correct drug-binding domain (highlighted in orange) on respective target proteins highly. In Q06187, the green domain ( PF00017 281 ) denotes the PROCYON-predicted binding domain, but the orange domain ( PF07714 402 ) is the correct binding domain. PROCYON predicts the binding domain as top-ranked in 24 examples, second-ranked in 5 examples, and so on. c) PROCYON can be finetuned to predict protein-peptide binding. Left, PROCYON is first finetuned on naturally occurring protein-peptide complexes from the Protein Data Bank (PDB), then tested on an experimental dataset of synthetic peptides screened for binding to the ACE2 protein. Right, the predicted binding scores for binders versus non-binders. Two-sided Mann-Whitney U test. d) Leveraging PROCYON to perform indication-specific drug target retrieval. In this example, the input consists of a novel task definition, the description of indications (nicotine addiction or major depressive disorder), and the name and structure of bupropion. PROCYON ranks known targets (norepinephrine transporter (NET), dopamine transporter (DAT), and nicotinic acetylcholinergic receptor (AChR)) of bupropion among the top 40/18,174 human proteins. Shown are 95% confidence intervals derived by perturbing words in the input prompt. ** p -value < 0 . 001 ; two-sided Wilcoxon signed rank test.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing a protein-domain language/model workflow and biomedical prediction results.

Panel a: Workflow schematic for protein O43451 (MGAM), with a 3D protein structure, orange-labeled binding domain, input prompt text about Miglitol, domain decomposition, and a ProCyon output table ranking protein domains with scores.

Panel b: Three example protein structures for target drugs Apixaban, Sirolimus, and Ibrutinib, each with predicted domain-score tables. A bar chart below shows the number of binding-drug examples by predicted domain rank, with most examples at Rank 1.

Panel c: ProCyon-Bind training/testing schematic. Training uses natural protein-peptide complexes; testing uses synthetic ACE2 peptide binders and experimental binding data. A violin plot compares predicted binding scores for “Peptide ACE2 binder” vs “Peptide ACE2 non-binder,” with binders visibly higher and a reported p value of 1.04e-4.

Panel d: Disease-drug information retrieval examples for “Smoking cessation” and “Major depressive disorder,” with prompt/input/output boxes for Bupropion and structure images. Bottom plots compare rank/attention-style information contributions labeled disease and drug information, suggesting model emphasis differs across disease/drug text.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 5: PROCYON characterizes poorly-annotated proteins and their functions. a) PROCYON generates phenotype predictions for AKNAD1. QA filtering selects the highest-confidence outputs; two of the three predicted phenotypes are experimentally supported. b) Additional PROCYON-generated phenotypes for other poorly characterized proteins. All proteins either have no UniProt-annotated function or have no UniProt function as of the PROCYON knowledge cutoff date. c) External evaluation of PROCYON using perturbation datasets. Parallel pathway analysis on genetic perturbation data is used to validate PROCYON-predicted functions for uncharacterized proteins. d) Top 100 functions prioritized by PROCYON for each protein. Percentile refers to the percentile of that protein among all 18,174 human proteins in our database for the specific function query. Green dots indicate overlap with perturbation-derived pathways; grey dots indicate other predictions. ** p < 0 . 005 , * p < 0 . 05 ; hypergeometric test. e) PROCYON-generated pathways for poorly characterized proteins associated with Parkinson's disease (PD). Left, heatmap of enrichment scores for each pathway compared to established PD-related proteins ('PD assoc.'), proteins expressed in the nervous system but not in PD or other neurodegenerative conditions ('Neuro control'), and proteins not expressed in brain tissues ('General control'), respectively. Right, differences in enrichment scores between 'PD assoc.' and 'Neuro control' and 'General control'. Statistically significant differences shown in green. Pathways are grouped by PD association score provided by human experts (right).

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure describing and evaluating **ProCyon**, a protein function/phenotype prediction system.

Figure type: workflow schematic plus benchmark/example panels with plots and heatmaps.

Visible panels:
- **a**: User input workflow showing a protein sequence/structure passed through “ProCyon” to generate phenotype/function descriptions, with QA filtering and supporting evidence such as subcellular localization microscopy and single-cell expression enrichment.
- **b**: Example generated annotations for proteins such as LYRM2, ANKDD1A, and UQCC4 compared with UniProt function text; includes checkmarks for apparent matches.
- **c**: Experimental validation workflow: CRISPRi perturbation of proteins, phenotype measurement, pathway analysis, and comparison to ProCyon-retrieved pathways.
- **d**: Dot/interval plot with x-axis labeled **Percentile**, showing several proteins ranked near high percentiles, with significance stars.
- **e**: Large pathway/phenotype comparison panel. Rows are generated phenotypes such as proteasome-mediated catabolism, lysosomal transport, oxidative stress response, vesicle-mediated transport, ATP transport, protein kinase activity, cell population proliferation, nucleotide metabolism, transcription regulation, extracellular matrix assembly, epigenetic regulation, and spermatogenesis. Includes an enrichment score heatmap and bar plots comparing **PD association** against neuro and general controls. A legend maps human expert score from 0 “Not associated” to 3 “Strong association.”

Main visible finding: ProCyon appears to generate biologically meaningful protein phenotype/pathway annotations that align with existing UniProt annotations, experimental CRISPRi pathway readouts, enrichment analyses, and human expert association scores.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: Training dynamics define distinct generalization regimes in biological reasoning models. We compare backbone choice, continued pre-training (CPT), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL) across genomics, transcriptomics, and protein tasks, and evaluate each stage on biologically meaningful in-domain (ID) and out-of-domain (OOD) splits.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model overview figure. It has four labeled vertical panels: **Backbones**, **Training Stages**, **Biological Modalities**, and **Evaluation**.

It shows general-purpose LLM backbones (**Qwen3-1.7B**, **Qwen3-4B**, **Gemma4**) and biological foundation models for **DNA: Evo 2**, **RNA: TranscriptFormer**, and **Proteins: ESM3**. The training pipeline includes **continued pre-training (CPT)**, **supervised fine-tuning (SFT)**, and **reinforcement learning (RL)**. The biological task modalities are **DNA pathway prediction**, **RNA drug target identification**, and **protein function prediction**, illustrated with sequence tokens and simple biological diagrams. The evaluation panel distinguishes **in-domain (ID)** and **out-of-domain (OOD)** settings and lists findings that SFT improves in-domain reasoning, RL enhances out-of-domain performance, and there are trade-offs across stages.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2: Supervised fine-tuning improves in-domain performance but reduces out-of-domain robustness. As SFT compute increases, ID performance continues to improve, while OOD performance peaks early and declines, indicating over-specialization to the training data. DNA/ RNA mean and std. over 3 random seeds (we only use one seed for Proteins, due to the size of the dataset).
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel line plot showing model performance across SFT epochs. Three panels are labeled DNA, RNA, and Proteins.

- DNA and RNA panels: y-axis is Accuracy, x-axis is SFT epochs with ticks 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.
- Proteins panel: y-axis is Fmax, x-axis is SFT epochs.
- Legend compares Qwen3-1.7B ID-Test, Qwen3-1.7B OOD-Test, Qwen3-4B ID-Test, and Qwen3-4B OOD-Test, with blue/orange lines and solid/dashed styles.
- Main finding: performance rises sharply after early SFT epochs, generally peaks or plateaus around 4-16 epochs, then slightly declines or stabilizes by 32 epochs. The 4B model is usually higher than the 1.7B model, especially for RNA and protein results.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3: Increasing data improves generalization more reliably than increasing SFT epochs. Scaling dataset size yields gains in both ID and OOD performance, but with diminishing returns, in contrast to the overfitting behavior observed when scaling epochs.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Two-panel line plot comparing model performance across training dataset sizes. Panels are labeled `ID-test` and `OOD-test`. The x-axis is `Training dataset size (K)` with values up to 20K; the y-axis is `F_max`. Legend shows `Qwen3-1.7B` in blue and `Qwen3-4B` in orange.

Main visible finding: `Qwen3-4B` consistently achieves higher `F_max` than `Qwen3-1.7B` on both ID and OOD tests, with performance generally increasing as training data size grows. The OOD panel shows a larger gap between models, with `Qwen3-4B` reaching about 0.31 while `Qwen3-1.7B` remains around 0.22.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 4: Reinforcement learning consistently improves out-of-domain robustness. Starting from strong SFT checkpoints, RL increases both ID and OOD performance, with the largest gains in OOD and diminishing returns after the first few epochs. DNA/ RNA mean and std. over 3 random seeds (we only use one seed for Proteins, due to the size of the dataset).
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Three-panel line plot comparing model performance across RL epochs for different test settings. Panels are labeled **DNA**, **RNA**, and **Proteins**. The x-axes show **RL epochs**; the DNA/RNA y-axes show **Accuracy**, and the Proteins y-axis shows **Fmax**. Legend entries include **Qwen3-1.7B ID-Test**, **Qwen3-1.7B OOD-Test**, **Qwen3-4B ID-Test**, and **Qwen3-4B OOD-Test**, with blue/orange and solid/dashed lines.

Main visible finding: performance generally improves with RL epochs, with the 4B model outperforming the 1.7B model across panels; ID-test curves are higher than OOD-test curves. Protein Fmax rises strongly by epochs 2-4 and then plateaus or slightly declines.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 5: Continued pre-training improves the effectiveness of downstream post-training. CPT improves both SFT and RL performance, with the largest gains appearing after RL and in out-of-domain settings.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Bar plot with four panels comparing accuracy across model/training variants for DNA and RNA tasks. The y-axis is Accuracy, ranging roughly 0 to 1.0. The x-axis categories are Base, SFT, RL, CPT+SFT, and CPT+RL. Panels are labeled DNA ID-test, DNA OOD-test, RNA ID-test, and RNA OOD-test. A legend compares Qwen3-1.7B in blue and Qwen3-4B in orange.

Main visible finding: accuracy generally improves from Base to SFT/RL and is highest for CPT+RL across DNA and RNA, with Qwen3-4B often slightly outperforming or matching Qwen3-1.7B. RNA Base performance is especially low, while SFT/RL and CPT variants substantially improve it.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 6: Stronger backbones improve performance achievable with post-training but preserve training dynamics. G-R does not display an initial drop in performance when starting RL, unlike Q1-R and generally performs better OOD. Mean and std. over 3 random seeds.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Two-panel line plot comparing RNA accuracy across training epochs. Both panels are titled “RNA.”

Left panel: x-axis “SFT epochs” with ticks 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32; y-axis “Accuracy” from about 0.2 to 1.0. Multiple model/dataset curves are shown with a legend, including Qwen3-1.7B and Gemma4-E2B variants for ID-Test, OOD-Test, and OV-Test.

Right panel: x-axis “RL epochs” with ticks 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16; y-axis “Accuracy.” The same model/test split curves are shown.

Main visible finding: accuracy improves rapidly after early SFT epochs, especially for higher-performing OOD/OV curves, while RL curves show a small initial dip around epoch 1 followed by recovery and gradual improvement. Orange Gemma-related curves appear highest overall, near ~0.9 accuracy by later epochs, while blue Qwen ID/OOD curves remain lower.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 7: Optimal adaptation requires asymmetric capacity across training stages. Higher LoRA rank benefits SFT, while lower rank is sufficient for RL, indicating that different stages require different adaptation capacity (both for ID and OOD tasks). Shown are results for drug target identification (RNA) tasks.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Heatmap-style experiment result with four panels comparing model performance across LoRA rank settings.

Figure type: grid of annotated heatmaps.

Panels: `Qwen3-1.7B — ID-test`, `Qwen3-1.7B — OOD-test`, `Qwen3-4B — ID-test`, and `Qwen3-4B — OOD-test`.

Axes: x-axis is `RL LoRA rank` with values 4, 16, 64; y-axis is `SFT LoRA rank` with values 256, 64, 16.

Quantity shown: numeric performance scores in each cell, likely evaluation accuracy or related metric for different supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning LoRA rank combinations.

Main visible finding: higher scores occur for ID-test than OOD-test, and the `Qwen3-4B` model outperforms `Qwen3-1.7B`. Across panels, RL LoRA rank 16 often gives the best or near-best score, while rank 64 is generally lower.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 8: Under a fixed post-training budget, a small amount of SFT followed by more RL gives the best ID-OOD trade-off. Across DNA and RNA, 1-3 SFT epochs followed by larger RL budgets generally give the strongest OOD accuracy, while larger SFT allocations achieve better ID performance.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Two-panel line plot comparing model accuracy across SFT/RL training epochs for DNA and RNA tasks. The y-axis is Accuracy, and the x-axis is labeled “SFT / RL epochs” with epoch pairs from 0/8 to 8/0. Panels are titled DNA and RNA.

The legend shows four model/setting curves: Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-1.7B OOD, Gemma4-2B, and Gemma4-2B OOD. Solid lines appear to be in-distribution results and dashed lines OOD results.

Main visible finding: DNA accuracies are generally higher and more stable than RNA. For DNA, solid curves peak around early-to-mid epoch settings near 3/5 or 4/4, while OOD curves stay lower around ~0.7-0.8. For RNA, Gemma4-2B peaks near 4/4 then declines, while Qwen3-1.7B drops mid-training and rises sharply at 8/0; OOD RNA performance remains lower and declines toward later settings.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 9: RL shifts the ID-OOD frontier across modalities. Each point is a trained checkpoint; color denotes training stage and marker shape denotes backbone. RL generally improves OOD performance at comparable ID performance across DNA, RNA, and protein tasks.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scatter plot comparing in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance across modalities/tasks. Three panels are labeled: **DNA (Pathway Prediction)**, **RNA (Drug Target ID)**, and **Proteins (Function Prediction)**. 

Axes show **ID Accuracy vs OOD Accuracy** for DNA and RNA, and **ID Fmax vs OOD Fmax** for proteins. A dashed diagonal indicates equal ID/OOD performance; a pale red shaded lower-right region highlights degradation under OOD conditions. The legend includes model variants: **SFT-only**, **SFT+RL**, **Qwen3-1.7B**, **Qwen3-4B**, and **Gemma4E2B**.

Main visible finding: most points fall below the diagonal, indicating lower OOD than ID performance. **SFT+RL** points generally appear higher than **SFT-only**, especially in DNA and protein panels, suggesting improved OOD performance for RL-tuned models.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 10: Optimal adaptation requires asymmetric capacity across training stages. Higher LoRA rank benefits SFT, while lower rank is sufficient for RL, indicating that different stages require different adaptation capacity (both for ID and OOD tasks). Shown are results for pathway prediction (DNA) tasks.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Heatmap-style experimental result with four panels comparing LoRA rank settings. Panels are labeled `Qwen3-1.7B -- ID`, `Qwen3-1.7B -- OOD`, `Qwen3-4B -- ID`, and `Qwen3-4B -- OOD`. The x-axis is `RL LoRA rank` with values 4, 16, 64, and the y-axis is `SFT LoRA rank` with values 16, 64, 256. Each cell shows a percentage performance value.

The figure measures model performance across combinations of SFT and RL LoRA ranks for two Qwen3 model sizes under in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings. Main visible finding: Qwen3-4B generally achieves higher percentages than Qwen3-1.7B, with many values around 95-99%, while Qwen3-1.7B OOD is lower, especially at smaller ranks.

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel schematic figure showing an RVQ-Alpha model workflow and downstream single-cell analysis tasks.

Figure type: conceptual workflow/model architecture plus task overview diagram.

Panels and labels:
- Panel a: “Data Encoding Pipeline” converts “scRNA-seq Data” through “RVQ Encoder” into “Discrete Tokens” and “Multi-Task Instruction.” These feed an “RVQ-Alpha Model” trained with “Pretrain & SFT & RL.” The right side shows an “MLLM Architecture” using “Diverse Single Cell Data” with “LLM” and “RVQ” components producing capabilities labeled “Understanding,” “Generation,” and “Reasoning.”
- Panels b-d: “Downstream tasks” grouped into “Single Cell Task,” “Cell Population Task,” and “Cell Perturbation Task.”
- Panel b includes cell type identification, top-K gene identification, gene expression generation, and batch effect correction.
- Panel c includes homogeneous cell type identification, heterogeneous cell type identification, and homogeneous phenotype identification.
- Panel d includes gene expression change prediction and differentially expressed genes prediction.

Visible biological/model quantities: scRNA-seq-derived cell/gene information, discrete RVQ tokens, cell types, gene expression, perturbation response, batch effects, and differential gene expression.

Main visible finding/message: the figure presents RVQ-Alpha as a multimodal large language model architecture that tokenizes single-cell RNA-seq data and supports multiple downstream single-cell, cell population, and perturbation prediction tasks.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2: Core dual-tokenization architecture. Text instructions are processed by a BPE tokenizer (top), while gene expression data passes through the RVQ tokenizer (bottom). Both token streams are fused at the LLM layer ( p ( t | h , c ) ), enabling bidirectional encoding and decoding: the BPE and RVQ detokenizers reconstruct the original modalities from the unified representation.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture schematic for tokenizing single-cell biomedical data with LLMs. The figure has two parallel input streams: “Meta data” processed by “BPE Tokenize” into a words vocabulary, and “Expression data” processed by “RVQ Tokenize” into a single-cell codebook. Both produce “Single Cell Discrete Tokens” that are passed into an LLM block. The output tokens are then decoded by “BPE Detokenize” back to metadata text and “RVQ Detokenize” back to expression data. Labels include “Words Vocabulary,” “Single Cell codebook,” “LLMs,” “Meta data,” and “Expression data.” The main message is a multimodal single-cell representation pipeline that converts textual metadata and gene-expression profiles into discrete tokens for language-model processing and reconstruction.

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture diagram for an automated answer-evaluation or reasoning-quality assessment system. It shows an input block containing “answer” and “metadata,” followed by a “Rule & Safety Guard” with hard constraints, prompt injection defense, and rule penalties. The pipeline then feeds a “Dual-Judge Semantic Engine” with an answer judge and conditional reasoning judge.

A lower expanded module shows template matching via regex/scanner, a semantic mapping engine comparing predicted label vs ground truth with categories “Exact Match,” “Vague/Directional,” and “Unrelated,” plus an electronic switch that triggers an audit hub. figure_candidates.caption: Figure 5: Per-dataset cell type accuracy across models. Bar-chart comparison of RVQ-Alpha (built on a Qwen3-4B backbone with the chosen ( Nc = 8, C = 32 ) RVQ tokenizer and GSPO reinforcement learning) against LangCell, Cell-o1, and C2S-Gemma2-2B on 8 evaluation datasets. Sampling budget: RVQ-Alpha uses pass@8 (8 stochastic decodings, best-of-8 selected by LLM judge); baselines use pass@1 (single-sample predictions from released checkpoints). This asymmetry favors RVQ-Alpha; see §5.2 for discussion. RVQ-Alpha wins on A013 (49.4%), D095 (80.9%), D096 (54.4%), and D102 (47.8%); Cell-o1 wins on D094 (37.4%); C2S-Gemma2-2B wins on D099 (64.3%), D101 (34.7%), and D103 (96.0%; see §7 for a training-data overlap caveat). LangCell is the weakest model on every dataset, peaking at 27.2% on D096. Baseline selection criteria are described in §4.6.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 6: Per-dataset Lowest Common Ancestor Distance (LCAD; Eq. 24) across models. Lower is better: LCAD measures the unweighted edge distance between predicted and ground-truth cell types along is-a relations in the Cell Ontology DAG [53, 10]. Sampling budgets are identical to Figure 5: RVQ-Alpha at pass@8, baselines at pass@1. RVQ-Alpha achieves the lowest mean LCAD on A013 (2.40) and D095 (2.22); C2S-Gemma2-2B leads on four datasets (D096, D099, D102, and notably D103 with LCAD = 0.39). figure_candidates.caption: Figure 11: RVQ embedding space by cell type. t-SNE visualization with perplexity 50 of LLM input embeddings for RVQ-encoded cells. For each cell, the 8 codebook embeddings from the model's expanded vocabulary are averaged to produce a single cell-level representation (26 cell types, N = 1,601 cells). Biologically related cell types cluster together: Neuron ( n = 366, upper right) forms a distinct cluster; immune subtypes (CD4+ T, n = 204; Myeloid, n = 201; T/NK, n = 117; CD8+ T, n = 83) overlap at center-left; epithelial types (Enterocyte, n = 58; Goblet, n = 18) form compact clusters. Sankey/alluvial flow plot showing cell type misclassification errors as raw counts. The left side is labeled “True Cell Type” and lists immune cell categories such as γδ T cell, regulatory T cell, plasmablast, natural killer cell, naive/effector/central memory CD4 and CD8 T cells, monocytes, and B cell subsets. figure_candidates.caption: Figure 13: Semantic confusion matrix for homogeneous tissue-type classification. Companion to the cell-type confusion matrix in Figure 10. A 10 × 10 heatmap covering Ileum, Colon, PBMC, Entorhinal Cortex, Adrenal Gland, Lymph Node, Chest Wall, Neck, Liver, and Nose (the converged GSPO tissue policy; best-of-32 sampling; offline evaluation judge threshold 0.75, the tissue-population operating point of §4.5; external test sets D101, D102, and D103, defined in §4.5). The largest off-diagonal cell is Colon → Ileum (1,294), with a smaller reciprocal Ileum → Colon (519), reflecting mutual confusion between gut tissues. Chest Wall, Neck, and Liver have diagonal zeros-Liver acts as a catch-all incorrect prediction for several rare tissues (receiving Ileum → Liver 361, Colon → Liver 242, PBMC → Liver ∼ 200), absorbing mass it never correctly predicts itself. The gut-tissue dominance and Liver sink pattern are consistent with the training data's tissue frequency distribution.

Measured/shown quantities: numbers of samples, spots, and image patches across biomedical datasets; sample distribution across tissue/cancer types.

Main visible finding: the model is trained/aligned using large-scale histology/image and spatial transcriptomics-related datasets, then evaluated or applied to temporal, 3D-spatial, and multi-omics downstream analyses.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Figure type: workflow/model architecture panel for a spatial transcriptomics prediction model. It is labeled “b. Model Architecture and Training Procedure.”

Visible panels/labels: H&E imaging and spatial sequencing inputs feed into an Image FM and ST FM feature extraction pipeline. A contrastive learning block shows a similarity matrix, followed by “Conv & Concat,” a FiLM module, and “ST Prediction” output. A legend marks gray arrows as input, green arrows as output, flame icon as trainable, and snowflake icon as untrainable. Lower inset panels show Image FM finetuning from DINO V2 using TCGA, GTEx, and in-house data, and ST FM finetuning from a Single Cell FM using HEST1K.

Biological/model quantity shown: the model predicts spatial transcriptomics from histology-derived image features and spatial transcriptomics foundation-model features, with diameter feature extraction scales shown as 2 µm, 55 µm, and 150 µm.

Main visible finding/message: the panel presents a multimodal architecture where H&E image features and spatial sequencing features are contrastively aligned, combined through convolution/concatenation and FiLM conditioning, then used to generate spatial transcriptomics predictions.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel schematic/results overview labeled “c.” with title “H2O Results Analysis and Applications.” It shows six application panels: context-aware gene-expression prediction with a small heatmap labeled EPCAM, ACTA2, and n_genes; multi-modal informative clustering shown as colored point clusters; cell-cell communication shown as a network graph with highlighted nodes/edges; temporal continuity shown as a line plot with x-axis tick marks around 0.1-0.4 and y-axis values up to about 25; spatial contiguity shown as a 3D tissue/block rendering; and multi-omics integration comparing “Spatial Transcriptome” and “Spatial Proteome” image-like maps. SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel biomedical results figure comparing spatial gene-expression prediction methods across datasets. Panels include boxplots of PCC for methods H2O, OmiCLIP, DeepPT, HistoGene, and BLEEP on ccRCC, PRAD, and IDCLymphNode; horizontal bar charts labeled “Best Gene Prediction Count”; a per-gene PCC comparison plot between H2O and the best competing result; a ranked “PCC Gap” gene plot; an enrichment-style bar chart with `-log10(P-value)` terms; and spatial expression heatmaps.

Measured quantity is mainly prediction performance using Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) and normalized gene expression across tissue spots. The visible finding is that H2O generally shows higher PCC distributions and the largest number of best-predicted genes across datasets, with spatial maps appearing closer to ground truth than competing methods for several marker genes.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel biomedical figure showing spatial transcriptomics / spatial domain and cell clustering results, t-SNE embeddings, and ligand-receptor interaction analyses.

Panels include:
- **a.** Spatial maps labeled **ST**, **Spatial Domain Recognition Image FM**, and **H2O**, with categorical color legends.
- **b.** Horizontal bar plots comparing methods, with H2O scoring higher than Image_FM, values around **0.66 vs 0.34** and **0.63 vs 0.44**.

- **e.** Spatial ligand-receptor interaction/network visualization over tissue spots, including zoomed regions with arrows labeled **L: MIF, R: CD44** and **L: MIF, R: CD74**.
- **f.** Spatial component map and stacked bar chart of ligand-receptor counts, with legend listing many components and text box reporting **198 ligands**, **371 ligand/receptor genes**, and **1036 ligand receptors**.
- **g.** Bar plot of **Pattern Abundance (#)** for ligand-receptor patterns, with top terms involving **MIF-CD44** and related interactions.

Main visible finding: the H2O method appears to better reproduce and refine spatial domains/cell clusters than Image_FM, and identifies spatially organized ligand-receptor interaction patterns dominated by MIF-related pairs.

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow schematic/biological diagram. It shows a developmental timeline from embryo/fetal stages through delivery and early postnatal stages, with tissue sampling indicated by vertical section-like strips beneath timepoints. Arrows lead to a droplet labeled “H2O” containing stylized cells/spot arrays, then to a grid heatmap labeled “Predicted ST Expression.” No numeric axes or legend are visible. The figure appears to depict predicting spatial transcriptomics expression across developmental samples using an intermediate water/droplet-based representation or model workflow.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Box-and-whisker plot panel labeled “b.” titled “Pearson of Genes from Cytokines.” The x-axis is labeled “Gene” and lists cytokine-related genes including CCL19, CCL2, CCL4, CCL5, CD40LG, CX3CL1, CXCL10, CXCL14, CXCL9, IL1B, IL1RN, IL3, IL7R, and SPP1. The y-axis is labeled “PCC,” indicating Pearson correlation coefficient values. A legend labeled “Age” compares two groups: “fet” in dark blue and “paed” in light gray.

Main visible finding: pediatric samples generally show higher PCC values than fetal samples for several genes, especially CXCL10, CXCL14, CXCL9, and SPP1, while CCL19 has the highest correlations in both groups.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel line plot figure showing temporal expression patterns for marker genes across developmental/timepoint labels on the x-axis: `12pcw`, `15pcw`, `16pcw`, `17pcw`, `18pcw`, `3mo`, `6mo`, `1.2yrs`, `1.6yrs`, `2.5yrs`. Panels are labeled with genes including `SPP1`, `COL12A1`, `KDR`, `MPP3`, `IGKC`, `CD19`, `VGF`, `MYT1L`, `TEF`, `RND2`, `PTGS2`, and `LIX1`.

The y-axes are not explicitly labeled, but the plotted quantities appear to be relative gene expression or activity trajectories over age/developmental stage. Red, blue, and gray traces likely indicate different gene groups or clusters. Main visible finding: different genes show distinct temporal trajectories, with some red genes higher prenatally and declining postnatally, while several blue and gray genes peak at specific developmental or postnatal timepoints.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow schematic/panel labeled “a.” showing a computational histopathology pipeline. It depicts a series of histopathology slide images, followed by image registration, then an “H2O” droplet icon suggesting spatial/omics or molecular profiling input, and finally a cube labeled “Predicted 3D tissue profiles.” There are no axes, plots, legends, or quantitative values visible. The main displayed idea is reconstruction or prediction of 3D tissue profiles from registered serial histopathology images and associated profiling data.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel 3D biomedical visualization, likely volumetric tissue or microscopy reconstruction. The panel is labeled “e.” and contains three side-by-side 3D renderings with coordinate axes labeled X Axis, Y Axis, and Z Axis. The subpanel labels are `LYZ`, `LYZ + ACTA2`, and `LYZ + ACTA2 + SPP1`.

The figure appears to show spatial distribution or co-localization of biological markers/proteins/genes in a 3D tissue volume. Gray/white structures form the main reconstructed volume, with the rightmost panel adding turquoise/green regions corresponding to `SPP1` signal or overlap with `LYZ` and `ACTA2`.

Main visible finding: adding ACTA2 and then SPP1 reveals additional internal marker-positive regions within the reconstructed tissue, with SPP1-associated areas appearing as scattered turquoise clusters embedded in or near the gray tissue structure.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel UMAP clustering figure from a biomedical single-cell/multimodal analysis. Four visible panels labeled around “h.” and “i.” show immune-cell embeddings:

- “Immune RNA Clusters”: UMAP scatter plot with axes UMAP1 and UMAP2, points colored by cluster labels 0-7.
- “Immune Protein Clusters”: UMAP scatter plot with axes UMAP1 and UMAP2, points colored by protein-derived cluster labels 0-5.
- “Immune WNN Clusters”: UMAP scatter plot with axes UMAP1 and UMAP2, points colored by WNN cluster labels 0-7.
- “Immune WNN Protein Weight”: UMAP scatter plot colored by a continuous protein-weight scale from 0.0 to 1.0.

The figure compares RNA-based, protein-based, and weighted-nearest-neighbor immune-cell clustering on the same low-dimensional manifold. The visible finding is that cluster structure differs by modality, while the WNN protein-weight panel shows spatially variable protein contribution across the embedding.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel UMAP feature-expression plot comparing RNA and protein measurements across immune cell marker categories. The figure has two rows labeled `RNA` and `Protein`, with five columns labeled `T Helper`, `Cytotoxic T`, `Regulatory T`, `Activated T`, and `B Cell`.

Each panel shows a UMAP scatter plot with axes `UMAP1` and `UMAP2`, colored by expression level using a blue-to-red color scale. Marker labels shown above panels include `CD4`, `CD8A`, `FOXP3`, `CD38`, and `CD40`.

The biological quantities shown are gene/RNA expression and corresponding protein abundance for immune markers. The main visible finding is that RNA and protein marker patterns differ across the same UMAP embedding: some markers show stronger or more localized protein signal than RNA signal, and expression patterns vary by immune cell type marker.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: Token analysis, BFT, and applications. a : Semantic composition of low-confidence tokens inside Group A (sparse-low) and Group B (dense-low). b : 4096-token trace illustrating one sparse-low window (Group A) and one dense-low window (Group B). c : BFT applies token- and sample-level loss adjustments. d : BFT-generated biomedical profiles are encoded by a text embedding model for downstream representation tasks.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure combining plots, schematic workflows, and model architecture.

- **Panel a:** Bar chart of **token composition (%)** comparing **Group A sparse-low windows** and **Group B dense-low windows**. Categories include interchangeable expressions, common vocabulary, biomedical entities, and causal/reasoning chains. Group A appears enriched for interchangeable/common vocabulary tokens, while Group B appears enriched for biomedical entities and causal/reasoning chains.
- **Panel b:** Line/trace plot of **4096-token response confidence**, with highlighted windows: **Window A sparse low-confidence** and **Window B dense low-confidence**. Zoom-in plots show token confidence patterns in each window, with local mean confidence annotated.
- **Panel c:** Workflow schematic for **Balanced Fine-Tuning (BFT)**. It contrasts token-level weighting for sparse low-confidence tokens in Group A with sample-level or trajectory-level weighting for dense low-confidence Group B, aiming to stabilize gradients and reduce overfitting.
- **Panel d:** Model pipeline diagram: an **LLM** plus **biomedical trajectory** undergoes **BFT** to produce **LLM-BFT**, which generates descriptions of biomedical entities and maps them through a text embedding model into an embedding space.

Main visible finding: low-confidence token regions are separated into sparse and dense patterns, with different token compositions, and the proposed BFT strategy weights them differently to improve biomedical entity description/embedding behavior.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2: Medical competence and biological process reasoning. a : Medical competence is measured across axis-wise (left) and theme-wise (right). b : Biological reasoning benchmark.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel quantitative plot figure with experiment results. Panel **a** shows grouped point/error-bar plots of **Score** across model sizes **14B, 32B, 70B**, split into **Axis** and **Theme** task categories. X-axis labels include biomedical/scientific concept categories such as dataset-related and semantic/theme categories. Legend compares methods: **Base**, **SFT**, **DFT**, **BFT-sample**, **BFT-token**, and **BFT**.

Panel **b** shows line plots of **Regent-1 Score** versus **Model Size** for benchmarks **MsigDB**, **NeST**, and **GeneOntology**, with separate rows/conditions and the same method legend. A green dashed horizontal reference line labeled **GeneAgent** is shown.

Main visible finding: **BFT variants, especially BFT/BFT-token in red/pink, generally improve scores over Base/SFT/DFT across model sizes and benchmarks, with larger models often scoring higher and approaching or exceeding the GeneAgent reference in some settings.**

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure comparing gene embedding/model methods.

Panel a: Three 2D scatter/UMAP-style plots labeled `scGPT`, `GenePT`, and `BFT`, showing gene categories as colored points. Legend includes gene biotypes such as protein_coding, lncRNA, miRNA, rRNA, pseudogene, IG_V_gene, TR_V_gene, snoRNA, snRNA, and others. The visible finding is that GenePT and BFT show more separated clusters by gene biotype than scGPT, where points appear more mixed.

Panel b: Bar charts of AUC performance for methods `scGPT`, `GenePT`, and `BFT`. Left chart is `Single gene input` with x-axis tasks including `TF range`, `Dosage sensitivity`, `Biased in male`, `Biased in female`, and `Bivalent in hPAs`. Right chart is `Multi gene input` with tasks `GDA` and `PPI`. BFT generally has the highest or near-highest AUC across several tasks.

Panel c: Bar charts of clustering performance. Left chart is `Clustering performance (phenotype)` with metrics `ARI`, `AMI`, and `ASW`; right chart is `Clustering performance (cell type)` with the same metrics. Methods compared are `PCA`, `scGPT`, `GenePT`, and `BFT`. GenePT/BFT appear stronger than PCA/scGPT on several clustering metrics, especially AMI for cell type.
